utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There was one preliminary to be raised by the Prosecution, if I am well informed. Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. There are actually two preliminaries, Your Honour. The first is just an update with respect to the CLSS review of the video-clips. It's not going to be completed today, and what I'd propose we do is mark the clips for identification and they would then be introduced once CLSS has had the opportunity to verify their accuracy, and if there are any errors in the transcripts we'll incorporate those corrections into them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't need the witness for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't need the witness for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so for that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, then -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the second issue had to do, Your Honour, with the Prosecution's position on Zvornik which Your Honour raised yesterday. And what I would propose to do in that respect is that it is our position that evidence relating to Zvornik is admissible, and in particular, in relation to counts 7 and 8 of the indictment and also to prove the JCE which is alleged to have commenced starting in October 1991. I have drafted some written submissions on those issues, Your Honours, and rather than to take up Court time I would propose to make written submissions which I could file on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess we will have to do written submission, Your Honour, although I note that neither Zvornik nor Bijeljina, the other topic that was the subject of the e-mail of last night, neither of those are on the Rule 65 ter summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the 65 ter summary issue, Your Honour, the issue of Zvornik is addressed at length in the witness's 92 ter statement which, according to the guidance, constitutes notice for the purposes of court and there is no need, according to the guidance, to amend the 65 ter summary, and the related clips to paragraphs 23 and 24 of the witness's amalgamated statement contain the references to Bijeljina. And this was also the subject of testimony from the witness in the Karadzic case which, obviously, has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having heard these observations and submissions, let's proceed. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I meanwhile use the time for the following: The Chamber would like to put on the record the correspondence concerning the comment chart presented to the witness yesterday. The Prosecution on the 25th of January had informally communicated a request to the Chamber to present Mr. Bell with this chart, and in informal communication on the 28th of January the Chamber had granted the Prosecution permission to do so as it did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. And Ms. Bolton will now continue her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I just wonder if we have the hard copy of the witness's statement available for him again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not aware of it being returned, but could we make sure that the witness has a hard copy of his statement. We can get started, I think. It's taken care of, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Let me remind you again of the importance of you and I pausing between question and answer. Now, near the end of your testimony yesterday, sir, you remarked that the Bosnian Serbs had heavy weapons in abundance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The microphone of the witness is not turned on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You had remarked about the Bosnian Serbs having heavy weapons in abundance. Could you comment briefly in the early part of the war on the Bosnian Muslims access to heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I could tell, the -- the Bosnian Muslims had very little access to -- to heavy weapons. The weapons, of course, were held in -- in arsenals throughout the former Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Serbs planned better and they had the access. And if I went, for instance, to see my friend who was in charge of the defence of Grbavica on the Serbian side of the lines, even there they had their own tank. They were well armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the video-clips you had the opportunity to review and which is the subject of a commentary in Exhibit P83 was a video you did on the fall of Foca in April of 1992. And in that video you remarked: "Until now, the two sides have lacked the heavy weapons to do this kind of damage to each other." Which warring party was using heavy weapons in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as I can tell, the fighting in Foca was done mostly with -- with light weapons. It was one of these places with -- with a wooden old town which incinerated very easily. I suppose at the very start of the war the heavy weapons were held by the JNA in their -- in their barracks, and at the very start of the war they were not used. Although, I remember quite early on being pinned down by gun-fire. This was sometime in May/June 1992 in the main street in Sarajevo, and there appeared to be some heavy weapons being used against us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to return to the siege, which is what we were discussing yesterday at the end of proceedings. I'm going to ask that you watch a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It is 65 ter 22509H, and I will ask in a moment for it to be played and to stop it at the 41 second mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Bell, is a video-clip that you discuss at paragraphs 84 to 86 of your statement describing visiting two batteries of mountain guns north-west of Pale in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So if that could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Early in the war he was named a war criminal by the Bosnian government which he resents. He never killed anyone he says in his whole life. Now he has it in his power to flatten Sarajevo from five miles away, with his 100 millimetre canon by direct or indirect fire. If it comes to a bombing of the Serbs as some Americans had suggested, his guns would be as prime a target for them as the city is for him."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We've paused the video at the 41 second mark and you can see two buildings in the foreground of the image before you. There is specifically in the centre of the screen a shorter white building and next to it a taller building that is blackened on top. Do you recognise those two structures?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a murky image but they look like the parliament building and the parliament office building, which was heavily damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And having personally visited the battery sites, can you comment, please, on the line of sight that Colonel Bartula had into the city from those positions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bartula had unusually for a battery commander a direct line of sight on the potential target, but he was adamant that he had not been using his guns. I gained access to this place with considerable difficulty. I had to describe myself as the head of the BBC delegation, I think. And he changed his mind and he gave us a very, I thought, moving account of his own emotions at being accused of being a war criminal in his own country. As I was trying to explain yesterday, it was very important to us, even at some risk to ourselves, to do as much as we could on that side of the lines. But I saw there was quite a lot of fighting going on around us, especially as darkness fell and it was small arms fire around the perimeter of the colonel's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Going back to my question, which was on the issue of the line of sight, you indicated Colonel Bartula had a direct line of sight. From where he was positioned, would he have been able to see where any shots he fired landed within the city and to make corrections, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not if they had landed on the -- the eastern part of the city. You get the view there of more of the central part. And it would be common for an artillery commander to have a forward observer, but he was so well-placed on that hill-side he didn't need one. He could see where -- if he wished to shoot he could see the target, most of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an associated exhibit. However, it's now been identified further by the witness, and I'd ask that it be marked for identification and admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we relying upon the audio? Because we were unable to follow the audio when it was being played. So if we are relying upon the audio, I would object. If we are not relying upon the audio, then I would not object.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was just a question of adjusting the volume in order to be able to hear the audio. I was able to hear it once I turned up my volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about translation, transcript? Do you rely on it; do you not? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We do rely on it, and it is one of the videos that is being reviewed by the CLSS who will determine the -- verify the accuracy of the transcript that is available, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what -- for the Chamber -- at this moment, let's MFI it and then see whether it's sufficiently -- if you want us to decide on a video-clip with audio, then at least we should know what it is before we can decide. And to say, Switch on your volume a bit higher and then you may hear it -- has the accused heard it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I didn't appreciate that other people were having difficulty hearing it. I don't know, obviously, whether General Mladic had any difficulty hearing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least we have it in the English language on the transcript. I don't know whether it was translated or not. You verify that and then at least you have an opportunity to give the transcript to Mr. Mladic for reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told on the B/C/S channel the translators said they were unable to hear it and they did not translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you discuss the matter with Mr. Mladic during the break, if you show him the English version of the transcript then you can come back and we will see how to resolve the matter, Mr. Ivetic. Madam Registrar, the video will be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video number 22509H received P835, Your Honours, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. You may proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I now wish to turn to the topic of attacks on civilians within the city of Sarajevo, and in that regard I wish to discuss a clip that is an associated exhibit to paragraph 72 of your statement. It's 65 ter 22531D.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am relying on the audio, Your Honours. Again it's being reviewed by the CLSS, and I'd be asking to play the first 34 seconds of this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, if a sound-track cannot be heard by the B/C/S interpretation, the Chamber would like to be informed immediately so that we can see what action can be taken so as to have a compete record. Please proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Sniper's corner, Sarajevo, as dangerous today as it has ever been. People taking a back road to work were open to sniper fire from Serbian positions in the hills. The Serbs had promised as part their new peace initiative that from now on they would be engaging only military targets. In this part of Sarajevo the promise was not kept, for these were civilians, in civilian vehicles, one of them with Red Cross markings."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to this clip you've just seen, sir, could you indicate, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I would like first to verify whether the audio was translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You have quoted somebody within the Bosnian Serb leadership as indicating that: "From now on," they would only be engaging military targets. Tell me if you recall who made that statement on behalf of the political or military leadership?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I don't have the privilege of seeing the video myself, though I heard the audio. At this distance, it would have been one of the leadership. It would have been Karadzic, Koljevic, or Zametica. But 20 years later, I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not sure what the difficulty is with the witness seeing the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not able to see that video, Your Honour, no. I am seeing the transcript unfolding before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- would we make sure that the witness and then look at the video. Could it be played again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be played again, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Sniper's corner, Sarajevo, as dangerous today as it has ever been. People taking a back road to work were open to sniper fire from Serbian position in the hills. The Serbs had promised as part of their new peace initiative that from now on they would be engaging only military targets. In this part of Sarajevo the promise was not kept, for these were civilians, in civilian vehicles, one of them with Red Cross markings."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, Your Honours, I'd be asking that this be tendered, MFI'd for confirmation by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22531D receives number P836, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, you describe at paragraph 50 of your amalgamated statement an occasion in January 1993 where a man was shot in the leg while attempting to gather water from standpipe in the basement of the maternity hospital, and it was an occasion when you drove that man to the hospital. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bolton. It was not actually in the maternity hospital. It was in the basement of a block of flats near the maternity hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you tells --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us if the individual who was injured, was this a case of somebody being caught in the cross-fire between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear to me that people -- they had to have water. It was the only standpipe working in the neighbourhood, and they were -- they were shot to and from this position where they could collect water. So I would not actually classify this as being caught in a cross-fire, I would classify this as being deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I don't know if you recall who was doing the targeting on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the victims were all on the government-held side, so common sense would tell me that the fire was coming from the other side, which was the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did civilians in Sarajevo take any steps in order to try to protect themselves from the dangers of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would say that the -- for the population of Sarajevo at that time, and this also applies to the Serb side, they were in the survival business and they would take whatever steps they could. They had no body armour. They had no armoured vehicles. They had to get out to gather fuel. Some of them were still working. They took whatever steps they could. On the upper slopes of Grbavica, on the Serb side, there was a road which was directly in the line of fire of snipers from the government-held side, and the people there had -- had --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, can I just interrupt you because, as you know, my time is limited, and I should have been more specific in my question. Could you tell me about measures taken by civilians in the Bosnian-held -- government-held territory to protect themselves from sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took whatever action they could, as we saw on that video-clip. They took back-ways. Sometimes they tunnelled out of the back of buildings to -- to find a safer way. They -- they ran. They drove as fast as they could. They carried their bicycles over waste land. They took whatever evasive action they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to turn to another topic you discussed in your amalgamated statement which is shelling of the city. And in particular, I am going to play you a chip that is associated to paragraph 83 of your statement. And this is an incident from January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could I ask that that clip, which I believe is 31 seconds, be played in its entirety. We will be relying on the audio, Your Honours, and I think it's an audio where you're going to need to turn it up a little bit to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you give the 65 ter number first.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. 22509G.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: In Sarajevo the horrors are not just heard of but lived through day by day. This is a particularly heavy bombardment of the old city. A single artillery shell fell on a queue of people waiting to pick up water outside the brewery. Eight were killed, 18 seriously injured. Of the dead, three came from one family, the mother and father who were killed instantly and the daughter who died later in hospital."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to that incident, sir, were you aware of any ABiH military activity in the area at the time of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. It was very much in the -- in the centre of the city. But it was not a war in which there were many easily identifiable military targets on the ABiH side of the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I was not during the entire time listening to the French translation, but there seemed to be a problem there. Could I hear from the French booth, and I'm on channel 5 now, what the problem was? Ms. Bolton, since you did not identify exactly where it is in the transcript, the French interpreters had problems in translation. Now if the B/C/S translation was there, the rights of the accused are observed. The French translation could be worked on after this, but may I urge you to be very precise in the information you give to all those who are assisting us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How close to the confrontation line was the brewery in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I would think it was about a third or half a mile.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, I'd ask that that clip be marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22509G receives number P837, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 81 of your statement you refer to being injured by shrapnel yourself from a mortar in August of 1992. And could you tell me where in the city you were at the time you were hit?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was near the -- the back road we used to take to avoid the dangers of sniper fire on the main road which meant being at the back of Marsal Tito barracks where the road make a kind of a detour around a loading platform. So we got on this loading platform, just open concrete, to try and actually get some idea of where the fire was coming from and what was going on, and I stayed out of cover too long and I was hit by this mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was there any ongoing military activity by the ABiH -- sorry, the Bosnian army at -- in proximity to your location at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were quite close to a United Nations base in the Marsal Tito barracks, but I saw no military activity going on around me except there was quite a lot of firing from unidentifiable sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've told us a little bit about civilians in Sarajevo and their -- the issues of shelling and sniping. Could you tell us whether there were other privations that civilians were subject to, particularly in the ABiH-held territory, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a war fought in the centre of a -- of an industrial city. For much of the time there was no electricity, there was no gas, there was no water, so people were living in very primitive conditions. And I was told some of the old people unable to leave the high-rises just died of hypothermia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I am looking at the clock. How much more time would you need because I think you had half an hour yesterday. You asked for one hour, and you're very close to half an hour now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'd checked with the Registrar at the end of the day yesterday and was told I'd used 23 minutes, and I have, I could indicate, Your Honour, probably about another 12 minutes to go. And again, we've had some issues today. I think I'm probably only around the 40-minute mark, 45-minute mark in the time I've used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, the Registrar keeps a record for reporting which is an administrative report which, sometimes, is based on, for example, the Chamber's questions or the Chamber's interventions even where the parties are fully responsible for that time. So I would like to keep that in my own hands. I'll ask Madam Registrar to give me further information. I'm asking it -- it is the Prosecution, I would think, who would very much like the witness to be concluded today. We had an early start. If you now use all the lost minutes and say, We are entitled to use them, then at the end the Defence will not be able to finish today. That's my concern. Would you please try to proceed as quickly as you can and as efficiently as you can. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, obviously during the conflict you filed a number of stories on behalf of the BBC which included coverage of targeting of civilians in the city by the VRS. Are you aware of whether anyone in the Bosnian Serb military or political leadership was keeping abreast of your reports?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The -- the Bosnian Serb leadership was extremely concerned about its public diplomacy. They -- they knew what was being broadcast because it could come back on the Euro Vision news exchange. And I remember somehow, Dr. Karadzic - maybe I gave it to him - he actually called the BBC 6.00 news, the early evening news directly, to protest about something that he had seen. He actually had the direct line number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Turning briefly to the issue of the report you filed on the shelling of the Markale marketplace in August 1995 which you describe at paragraph 104 of your statement, do you recall where you were when you became aware that a shelling had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was handing over to a colleague who had arrived the night before, and we were both attending the daily UNPROFOR news conference when we heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how long would it have taken you after hearing about the incident to actually get on scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how is it that you actually learned about the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Word got to the press conference somehow. I can't remember. We all stampeded out of the room and went as fast as we could to the scene of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wish to discuss very briefly modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I ask that we play 65 ter 22354, the first 34 seconds only. And we are relying on the audios, Your Honour. This is being reviewed by the CLSS, and it's referred to at paragraph 100 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... are involved in stand off with French UN peacekeepers; the Serbs laid mines around the disputed check-point on the airport road outside Sarajevo. There has also been an upsurge in fighting around Sarajevo and at Bihac between Bosnian Serbs and government troops. "Martin Bell: The cease-fire appears to be crumbling rapidly. Today there were offensives on at least two fronts in Bosnia and south of Sarajevo. The suburb of Hrasnica came under Serbian attack for the third successive day. A rocket leveled five house, killed one person, and injured several more. Outside ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the destructive power of the rocket that leveled the houses in Hrasnica, can you comment on how that compared with other weapons you had seen in Sarajevo up to that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In its explosive power this was the heaviest weapon that I had seen used. I think it was a 500-pound modified air bomb. All sides in this war were using whatever they could, and some of the -- those -- the Croats used to roll sea-mines down onto Muslim houses in Gornji Vakuf. But this was a extraordinary development and an indication of total breakdown of the cease-fire at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 101 of your statement, you indicate that the modified air bomb was disproportionate and has no chance of distinguishing between military and civilian targets. What did you mean by saying it couldn't distinguish between military and civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the extent of the blast and the destruction it could cause. Obviously it would depend on where the modified air bomb landed, but if it -- shall we say, if you were standing anywhere on a football pitch, you would be very lucky to survive. And we hadn't seen a single weapon as destructive as that at earlier stages in the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You refer at paragraph 100 of your statement to a modified air bomb attack on the TV building in July 1995. Could you tell us how often you visited that building?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited that building every day. We broadcast from there. We had an office there which we leased from the Bosnian television service. So it was our -- I wasn't actually able -- somebody else was covering for the BBC then, but the bomb exploded in the well. The television station was like a figure eight with straight sides and it fell into one of the wells in the building and caused extensive damage and some casualties both to Bosnians and to some of western journalists based there. I had a friend who nearly lost his eyesight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, you have four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Very quickly, sir, did you see any evidence in your visits to the TV building to suggest it was ever being used by the Bosnian government for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatever, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You describe in your statement an attack by Arkan's tigers in Zvornik in April 1992, and you also mention in your report that Arkan's Men had taken a number of Muslim extremists from Bijeljina into custody. Could you tell us how you recognised the men in the Zvornik area as Arkan's Men?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The image was shot by a friend of mine, Dragan Havzjevocic, who was based in Belgrade. I knew Arkan personally. I had met him a number of times, and it was definitely -- they had identifiable uniforms. They tended to wear balaclavas. And it was definitely Arkan who was saluting the Serbian flag as it was hoisted on the municipality in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you subsequently learn after events in Zvornik that Arkan's Men had been involved in an attack in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that but I didn't have a reliable account of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there media coverage of that attack, and if so, how widespread?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a famous still picture which ran on the front page of -- of "Time" magazine by a photo journalist called Ron Haviv and it was one of Arkan's Men with his boot on a head of a Muslim prisoner in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, sir, I'll ask that 65 ter 22619A be played for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, we would be relying on the audio, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: The United Nations here has all contact with the Bosnian Serbs. Yet the Serbs want to open talks with the contact group whose peace plan they have rejected about the hostages and about security guarantees. This may be an attempt to blitz their way back to the conference table but they do seek an end to their isolation. "The Serbs are not doing well militarily. They have called for volunteers to hold the line on one battle-field, and near Brcko they failed in an offensive to widen the corridor connecting the tow parts of their territory. They are also responding by tightening the noose on the capital. For the people here, it's like a return to the worst of times. The Serbs have cut off both power and water. The people of Sarajevo have been here before. They have learned to improvise and need all the best friends they can find. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, what did you mean in that report where you referred to tightening the noose around the capital?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city was under siege. The fighting was as intense as it had been in the first summer of the war. This was the third summer. There was no running water as you see from that. I think it was an attempt to force a negotiations on terms favourable to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And finally, sir, did events elsewhere in Bosnia have any impact on what happened in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but unfortunately our access was so limited both by the ABiH and, of course, we were cut off from the Serbs. And I had written about this, that we tended to report Sarajevo as if it were the whole of Bosnia which, of course, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could 65 ter 22619 be tendered and marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22619A receives number P838, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. And the previous video?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you, Your Honours. If that could also be marked for identification and introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the 65 ter number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22354 receives number P839, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That concludes our direct examination, Your Honours. Did you wish me to address the issue of the exhibits or should we leave that until the witness completes his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see whether we can conclude the witness's testimony. Mr. Ivetic, I tried to work out a schedule. You would have, I would say, almost all of the time remaining today. We'll take the first break at ten minutes past 10.00; we resume at half past 10.00. We'll take the second break at 25 minutes to 12.00; we'll then resume at 5 minutes to 12.00 until 1.00, and we resume at 20 minutes past 1.00 until quarter past 2.00. Mr. Bell, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Bell. Today I have several areas I would like to ask you some questions about to try and assist us to better understanding your testimony and to clarify some issues that you might have personal knowledge of. Before we begin, insofar as we both will be using English, we have to be mindful to observe a pause between question and answer for the interpreters. And by all means, even though we would both be using English, there might arise a time when one of my questions is not clear, please do not hesitate to bring that to my attention. Is that fair, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is fair, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would begin. First, I want to ask a few things relative to your background and experience. Prior to going to the former Yugoslavia in 1991, did you at that time speak any of the Yugoslav languages, or did you have to rely upon an interpreter when being deployed to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, in Slovenia, in Croatia, and in Bosnia, I relied on some very good interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have to at some time stop using Serbian interpreters, that is ethnic Serbian interpreters, because the Muslims refused to talk with you with a Serb translator present?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is true. I remember when it happened, quite early on in late April 1992, we went to Butmir on the far side of the airport to witness the distribution of United Nations aid, and the Muslims there insisted that my Serb interpreter who came from Belgrade, Vladimir Marionovic [phoen] was not allowed to accompany us. At that point I regretfully sent him back to Belgrade, though he continued to operate out of Pale with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I note that you left the BBC in 1997 and entered politics thereafter. Could you please explain for us the circumstances behind you leaving the BBC? Am I correct that there was some kind of disagreement with your bosses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, Mr. Ivetic, there was not. I was completing a documentary of Kofi Annan's first three months in office as Secretary-General of the UN. And I entered politics in rather odd circumstances. There was a -- there was a conservative MP who was suspected of being corrupt. He held a very safe seat and the two opposition parties were looking for someone outside politics to stand as an independent and to take him out or defeat him, and so I -- I was persuaded to stand, and I won, and I served in parliament for four years as an independent member.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I believe you have authored some books. In your statement, which we have before us, at paragraph 6, which would be P832, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for those following along it's page 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned one of these books, entitled "In Harm's Way," that dealt with events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you please identify the other books that have been published and the topics that are addressed in each?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I wrote a book about my experience in politics called "An Accidental MP." I wrote two books on international politics and war. "In Harms Way," was -- sorry, "In Harm's Way" was -- "Through Gates of Fire" was one, and "The truth that Sticks" was another. I wrote a book of poetry which was published last year, mostly about war and politics. And a new edition of "In Harm's Way" to mark the 20th anniversary of the start of the war where the new introduction was published in April of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I want to get back to the time-period when you departed the former Yugoslavia in 1991. And I want to ask you if prior to then or at that time you had performed any research into the events leading up to the recognition of the break-away Yugoslav republics of Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had, as it happened, done a television documentary back in the Tito time about Marshal Tito's 80th birthday, so I was familiar with some of the situations and some of the tensions underlying in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want to ask you also, did you have an existing news sources, that is to say sources or contacts, in the former Yugoslavia that you had cultivated prior to going over there, or did you have to rely upon making new connections with potential sources once you arrived on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I -- I -- I had to really make it up as I went along. I made connections, obviously, with the United Nations, with the European Community observers. I talked to local journalists. If you're a war reporter you have to learn rather fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to briefly ask you to explain something that you put in one of your earlier statements, the February 1996 statement, to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to do so I'd like to call that document up. It's 1D656 in e-court. And according to my notes it should be page 2 in both languages in e-court. And in the English the part that I will be asking about is the second paragraph from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd like to focus on the part of this selection that reads as follows: "Slovenia made the first step towards war with its declaration of independence. It did so for its own selfish purposes, but it was hard not to have foreseen the consequences elsewhere. The Croats could not hold back once the Slovenians went for it." And, sir, I want to ask you, what was your understanding of the selfish purpose that you have identified behind Slovenia's declaration of independence. Di it amount to an economic factor that they wanted to separate from the less prosperous remainder of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, I think you have correctly identified it. There were some serious economic problems, even before the death of Marshal Tito. And the wealthier republics, Slovenia and Croatia, resented being asked, as they saw it, to bail out the less wealthy, the Macedonians and the Kosovars and that was a cause considerable tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one more thing, sir, about the terminology used here that I would like to ask you about. When you say it was hard not to have foreseen the consequences elsewhere, did you mean by that not only that other republics would seek independence but that there might also be war that would erupt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, in my book "In Harm's Way" I talk about the law of unintended consequences and the -- some documents were passed to me by one of the international diplomats including Lord Carrington's expressed concern to the European Community that the unilateral recognition of Croatia would light the fuse to a war in Bosnia which, of course, is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and so just to finish up with the Slovenian issue, in your mind do the Slovenian authorities bear some responsibility for the wars that followed in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking for a judgement on a responsibility, Mr. Ivetic, and although I do appreciate that some opinions of this witness can be accepted, this is a question which goes too far. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now move on to a different but related topic. You have testified in prior cases, most notably the Perisic case at transcript page 3203 and the Karadzic case at transcript page 9805 about the so-called Genscher push for recognition. And I want to try and take a look at that and break it down so that we can all understand what you mean. First of all, sir, is this related to the actions of a German diplomat named Hans Dietrich Genscher?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was the foreign minister at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would like to call up a portion of the Karadzic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can have in e-court, please, document 1D00654. And when we get that document, I'll be looking for 52nd page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, this will be the transcript of the 14th of December, I believe, of 2010 and should correlate to transcript page 9805 of the -- of that transcript once it comes up. And I will be looking at the top of the page. And your answer is recorded as follows, sir, and if you could follow along with me: "A. Yes, Dr. Karadzic, I have argued repeatedly that -- as Lord Carrington did, that when the European Community agreed to the recognition of Croatia, it made war in Bosnia inevitable. Lord Carrington warned that it could well be the small spark that ignites the powder keg of Bosnia, and yet the European Community agreed to this. And when I lay the blame for what happened beyond the peoples and armies of Bosnia as the war developed, I believe that the western democracies, and specifically my own government, bear some burden of responsibility. In fact, I can tell you that after I left Bosnia, I fell into politics in the United Kingdom and became briefly a member of parliament, and this was one of my motivating forces. I thought, if this is how little politicians can do, maybe I can try to do better as a politician." First of all, sir, I have to ask you whether you stand by this portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you restart your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I have to ask you whether you stand by this selection from your testimony in the Karadzic proceedings as being truthful and accurate, and would you testify today similarly having taken the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I've also had the opportunity to discuss these events with Douglas Hurd, who was then the British foreign secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was Mr. Hurd of a similar view?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not. He defended the -- the -- the British -- I'll be as brief as I can. We -- there was a change of mind. The British were initially opposed to the recognition of Croatia but ten days before there had been a meeting about the Maastricht Treaty and the Germans had been very helpful to the United Kingdom on its opt-out clauses, and at the meeting on the recognition of Croatia, Hans Dietrich Genscher reminded Mr. Hurd of that helpfulness and Mr. Hurd then sought instructions from Downing Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe we are talking about the same meeting that I was just about to go through. Let me just double-check.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D648.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this will be a facsimile copy of your book "In Harm's Way." And if we can have page 3 of the document in e-court. And this should correlate to pages 36 and 37 of hard print version as we have not put the whole book into e-court. And I believe the events that you have just in part summarised begin at the middle of page 36 and the paragraph that has the text that begins, "The decision was taken on 16 December 1991 and" -- well, let me just read this section for you and see if there's any additional comments that you would like to make about this incident: "The decision was taken on 16 December 1991. The Germans were not in a mood to be outvoted. It was an issue that mattered more to them than to anyone else around the table. As a friend who observed their diplomacy from a privileged vantage point described it, 'Bonn believed that the act of recognition would somehow be like waving a magic wand over the problem.' But at the first vote only the Belgians and Danes were with them. Mr. van den Broek himself opposed them strenuously. Then something happened in the course of the ministerial dinner and before the final vote at 2.00 in the morning, which changed the minds of the reluctant nine, Britain and France included. The Germans prevailed. Much later, with the benefit of two years' hindsight of the consequences, it was characterised by one of the mediators as 'a damn near criminal decision.' It opened the way to a fateful referendum on Bosnia, and the declaration of an independent republic against the wishes of one of its constituent peoples. It left Bosna in a sort of limbo to be fought for and in effect condemned 200.000 people to death." Now, first of all, sir, with respect to this selection from your book, do you stand by what you wrote as being truthful and honest, and would you repeat the same today even having taken the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would with one exception, which is that the casualty total in the new edition of that book I put the total casualties at 98.000. We know what happened now at that dinner and that was the subject of my previous answer. And if it's any help, the diplomat quoted was Cyrus Vance's deputy, the late Herb Okun.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You had anticipated the questions I had in regard to that. I also want to ask you, do you have any insight as to -- you have already told us why the British authorities changed their vote. Do you have any insight whether, in fact, the British authorities then undertook to change the minds of the other member nations who had previously not voted in favour of the German resolution?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is that the United Kingdom, as one of the major players in what was then the 12 of the European Community, had much influence. And the others were quite happy to -- including the French, were then -- once the British were persuaded, the others were happy to fall into line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you had already --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will try to endeavour to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You had already mentioned warnings by Lord Carrington as to the potential for the recognition of these break-away republics igniting the powder keg. If we can return to the text, the top of page 37 on the right-hand side of the screen continues to give other details about the warnings that were made at the time. And I'd like to touch upon those briefly. So I would propose to read the first paragraph into the record and then ask you some follow-up questions about that, sir. It begins as follows: "If that seems too hash a judgement - what else were the Serbs, given their history and paranoia, expected to do? And to the argument that their reaction could not have been predicted, the answer is that it could have been, and was. It was predicted both by Lord Carrington and by the Secretary-General of the United Nations in their prescient letters to the European Community's Council of Ministers. It was predicted by the community's own monitors on the ground. And it was predicted by the British and German ambassadors in Belgrade in messages which were discounted at the time but will one day form part of the historical record. In the judgement of the American ambassador, 'War in Bosnia now became virtually inevitable.'" And, sir, I have to ask you, first, with respect to this selection from your book, do you stand by the words I have recited from there as being honest and truthful based upon your knowledge and would you repeat the same even today under the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I -- when I revised my book, I -- I made no changes in judgements whatever. Only in casualty figures, some were too high and some were too low.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to all these other sources of warnings that you have now identified in this selection, were those all matters that were known of record at the time, or are these things that have come to light only after the events of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a mixture of the two, Mr. Ivetic. Some of the -- some came to light like the reflections of the American ambassador, some I was aware of at the time, since I knew the British ambassador in Belgrade very well, and some were in documents passed to me at a conference on Bosnia while the war was still going on by the American diplomat, Herb Okun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the clock. We are close to the moment where we should take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will ask the witness to follow the usher. We will take a break of 20 minutes. I'd like to see you back after that. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, just while the witness is being brought in, I thought I'd just use the time to indicate I'd been asked to put on the record that the other witness who had been scheduled for this week, RM175, has obviously been rescheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, the next paragraph of the text of your book talks about the situation that you have already identified for us in court; namely, that the British representatives changed their vote due to a -- getting an opt-out clause for the Maastricht Treaty. The question I have for you is: Here you identify that this information, that is, the trade off between the opt-out clause in Maastricht and the British support for recognition of Croatia and Slovenia was verified by the independent witnesses, and I'd like to see if you could be a bit more specific as to the nature of these witnesses, either by position or any other identifying remarks that you could give us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber has considered during the break your line of questioning. The Chamber does not in any way -- ignores that the background of the history of the war on the Balkans has some relevance. At the same time, the Chamber notices that Mr. Mladic is not charged with a war having happened but for his responsibility for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide to be comitted. Now what we have heard during the first hour of your cross-examination, it was not an entire hour --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Was mainly about what seems not to be, at least in the view of this Chamber, seems not to be the matters from which we finally would have to decide. Now at the beginning of the second session you apparently are continuing that line of questioning, and the Chamber would like to clearly express that with full acceptance of some relevance of the background that it is still background and that core of the case is elsewhere. Would you please keep that in mind also in view of how you wish to spend and divide your times over the various subjects, also in view of the testimony given by the witness in chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I was just finishing up the last three or four questions I had on this matter that were interrupted by the break. Let me see if I can try and short-circuit the said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of the selection which we have just read, sir, you ask: "What else were the Serbs, given their history and paranoia, expected to do?" And I would like to just ask two questions relating to that aspect that you have now confirmed, and the first of which would be: In the course of becoming familiar with the history of the region, did you have occasion to learn of the Croatian puppet state that existed under the auspices of the German Nazi regime in World War II and that covered both present day Croatia and present day Bosnia-Herzegovina and the persecution and killings of ethnic Serbs by the Croat and Bosnian Muslim organs of that state?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Ivetic. I was well aware of this during my time in Croatia, which included a visit to the notorious Jasenovac concentration camp. I heard of it in my many dealings with Croats and, indeed, with Serbs, in Croatia and in Bosnia, and I've never in all my life reported a war in which the ordinary, average soldier on the ground, especially on the Serb side, was so well aware of his people's history and what he was fighting for. This was entirely new in my experience. So I got pretty well informed quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now in regards to some terminology that you I think used in testimony in other cases, I want to just clarify. In terms of these -- this World War II puppet state, am I correct that the Croat and Muslim armed groups that existed during that time-period and which were aligned with the Nazi Germany powers, that they were called the Ustasha movement and the SS Handzar movement respectively?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Ustasha movement that I was familiar with, and almost from the start of war in Bosnia, in Herzegovina, you would find Croats driving around with pictures of the Ustasha leader, Ante Pavelic, at the back of their car.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You have anticipated my question which was to transition to 1991 and your time in Croatia and in Bosnia in the years thereafter. I would like to ask you something specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at 1D657. This again -- I apologise, not again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is for the first time a statement that you signed for the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in October of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when we call up this exhibit, this document, I guess we should look on the first page first just to verify that it's the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the record, sir, is that your signature on the bottom right corner of the English version on the right-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could please have the fifth page of this statement in English and the fifth page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on the first paragraph on the page in the English, sir. And the selection I'd like to ask you about begins and reads as follows: "I also saw many 'HOS' signs in Vitez. HOS were dressed in black. Whatever control Blaskic had over HOS and Kraljevic, who was in charge of them, was fairly loose. Kraljevic was in control over one area in the front line with ABiH. Blaskic needed his help." And I'd like to stop there and ask you, first of all, sir, in regards to -- well, first of all, in regards to this selection from your statement which I've now read, do you stand by those words as truthful and accurate having in mind that you have now taken the solemn declaration before beginning your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would add that as well as ABiH at that time, the Croats in Vitez felt threatened by the Mujahedin who were, of course, allied to ABiH but not under their control. And the Blaskic case was an issue of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I want to ask you, first of all, the HOS signs and the HOS unit, are we talking about -- first of all, in respect of the signs, emblems that would feature a Croat chequer-board with a capital U symbol, that stood for "Ustasha"? Was that your experience?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the -- certainly the chequer-board this -- this stage, 20 years ago, 21 years ago, I can't remember the U.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe any of the signs that you say you saw in Vitez relating to the HOS?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember they were just spelling out the -- the three letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to learn that the HOS was affiliated with a particular political party, the Croatian Party of Rights, led by a man by the name of Dobroslav Paraga, who was advocating a resurgence of the World War II regime?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They also by then -- in the Croatian war, they had some British mercenaries fighting along side them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now this selection from your prior statement that we read relates to Vitez. For those that might be unfamiliar with geography, could you tells where Vitez is located?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic. Vitez was in the Lasva valley. It was a -- it was a Croat enclave. Vitez part of Gornji Vakuf and other villages roundabout. It was surrounded by -- by government forces. The HVO felt they were outnumbered and they particularly felt threatened by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to ask you, in your discussions with the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership and in your discussions with the common Bosnian Serb soldier throughout the time of your stay in the region to report on the conflict going on there, did these individuals often talk to you or refer to a fear of a resurgence of the Ustasha and Muslim Handzar movements from World War II?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic. These were matters regularly raised at all levels, and I think - and this is not a criticism at all - but I had written somewhere that from my experience the Serbs live their history like no other people on earth. And -- and they have every reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just one more question about the events in Croatia before moving on to the latter events in the neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree that what was happening in Croatia in 1991 and 1992 made people of all ethnic groups in Bosnia weary and made them start planning to defend themselves against the other ethnic groups, particularly those who had fought against them in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that, Mr. Ivetic, is both yes and no. Of all the republics of Yugoslavia, Bosnia was the one with the most mixed marriages. Still the most Tito'st, I would say, were the great reverence for the Marshal. And many people would just refuse to believe that the worst-case scenario was going to happen. I think the Serbs from their experiences of the Ustasha state were probably more aware of the dangers and they certainly prepared better for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is there major dispute about the matters which were elicited from this witness by Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think these historical events are exactly the kind of thing that the Prosecution would be willing to agree to. And if Mr. Ivetic were to put that into filing in compliance with the Chamber's guidelines, I think he would find that we would agree to most of what's been led here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, could you please keep this in the back of your mind when you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to now move on to another topic focussing on your deployment as a journalist to the republic -- to -- across the boundaries to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And specifically I want to start with the press corps that were in Sarajevo, and I want to address something that I think you've said in prior testimony. And to be fair I'd like to bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's 1D653 in e-court. And once that is located I'd like the 28th page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for your information, sir, this will be a transcript from, I believe, the Perisic proceedings, and it should correlate to transcript page 3192 of that proceeding's record of transcript. And on that page, I'd like to focus on lines 8 through 14, if I may. And now we have that on the screen, sir, I'd like you to follow along and then I will have some questions for you: "Q. Was everybody interested in the same sort of stories that you have described? "A. There was more of an agreed agenda than I think there is now. Yes, on the whole. There was no tabloid press there very much. I don't think there were any great differences between us in the way that we covered the story, except that I probably spent more time with the Serbs than most of the rest." And now the first question I have to ask you is, again, as a matter of formality, can you confirm and do you stand by this portion of your testimony from the Perisic case as being truthful and accurate and would you so testify again today if asked to do so given the solemn declaration that you have taken?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask for a little bit more detail and clarification. Could you explain for us a little more what you meant when you used the term "agreed agenda" in this context?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a more of a reference to the way that journalism has changed since that time. As the audiences have fragmented and there is, in my experience, less concentration on foreign news than there was at that time, there were some very serious journalists there. Some very good friends. We were a close-knit group. And we worked as a team. That's all I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to your observation your comment that you probably spent more times with the Serbs than the rest of your colleagues, would you agree with me that this means that the -- that the other journalists were primarily reporting from just one side, that would be the Bosnian government side, of the conflict line?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was -- that was my perception at the time. And, of course, by the end of the war we were all driven back and I could no longer have access to the -- to the Serb held areas. But I believed then that the Serbs were absolutely crucial to the -- to finding an outcome. And I spent a lot of time and I wasted a lot of time and I risked my own life and the lives of those with me to cross those front lines and meet those Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, your fellow reporters from the Sarajevo press corps, am I correct that they sort of labeled you as being pro-Serb merely because you wanted the venture over and see the other side and spent more time with the Serbs than they did?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never actually said so publicly, Mr. Ivetic, but they -- they -- I got the impression that they felt I was wasting my time. And for some of them, this was a -- this was a black and white issue, whereas to me it was always etched in shades of grey. And if I had the war again, I'd do the same thing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you, during that time-period when you were reporting from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, am I correct that the editors back home had already early on gotten themselves into a mindset of the Muslims being the good guys and the Bosnian Serb side as being the bad guys in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic. I was aware of this mindset on the occasion of the notorious ambush of the JNA column during the UN brokered exchange between General Kukanjac and President Izetbegovic. And the following morning I saw the shot-up ambulance, and I told my editors what I was going to report about, and they said, Are you sure? I said, Yes, I am sure. I talked to a colonel who survived it. And then they accepted it. But there is a department of preconceived notions in journalism, as in other walks of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I'd like to move along and call up 1D648 and turn to page 16 in e-court of the same which would correlate to page 129 of the hard copy text, I believe. And that's on the bottom side of the right-hand side of the screen. And it bleeds over to -- or spills over to the next page. And I'd like to present this to you and ask you some more questions about these observations, sir. So if you would be so kind as to follow with me I will begin: "This may seem a partizan account, as if we were taking sides with beleaguered Muslims. Many journalists did, which was perhaps the flaw in the generally crusading character of the Sarajevo press corps. But the Serbs, in their section of the city, led almost as miserable a life. They too were sniped at and mortared and wounded, though generally not under the eye of the TV camera. Their civilians were also in the line of fire. And contrary to the general belief, they were not all wild men from the mountains. One of their front line warriors, where the Grbavica salient reached deepest into the city centre, had been a judge before the war, in the old multi-ethnic order of things. 'We are living here,' he said. 'This part of Grbavica has been our home. It is a question of knowing why you are fighting. If the lives of the members of my family are endangered, and someone is going to cut my throat because I am a Serb, then I really do not care whether I have a knife, a gun, or a cannon, but I shall use it.' "The Serbs seemed to model themselves on the old western gun-slinger, Wild Bill Hickok, who was said never to have killed a man except in self-defence, but to have spent a great deal of his time defending himself. And the Serbs weren't waiting to be attacked. They got their retaliation in first." The first question I have for you first, sir, is: With respect to this selection I have read, is this a truthful and accurate account and would you so repeat today subject to the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it your experience that the Serb soldiers around Sarajevo were all locals who in their mind were fighting for the defence of their own homes and their own families?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was generally the case. I vividly remember, Your Honours, one doesn't expect to see judges in the front line of a war, but there he was. And as I was explaining before, they could all, at whatever level, give a good account of why they were doing what they were doing. But in the course of the war, I also discovered there were some units coming in from outside, from Belgrade, former JNA, but predominantly the soldiers in the front line were indeed local people mobilised by the -- for the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the beginning of this selection from your book which I read, you talk about many journalists did take sides with the beleaguered Muslims. I'd like to ask you, how prevalent was this bias in the Sarajevo press corps that you mentioned here? Approximately what percentage did take sides with the Muslim side that was viewed as being beleaguered?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not so much a case of consciously taking sides as of not going anywhere outside the government held parts of Sarajevo and seeing the war from that perspective, and some of them were very comitted. A friend of mine said, "This is our Vietnam." Well, Vietnam was my Vietnam and I'd been in eight wars before I came to this one, so I tried to bring some experience to bear. But towards the end of the book you've quoted from, I lament that so much of the reporting at the end of the war was done on an axis of a mile and a half, shall we say, from the airport to the old Turkish fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And would these comments that you've made about the limited nature of the movements and reporting of other journalists be true for the entirety of the period or would it be earlier in the period or later in the period?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- the -- because of field security, which is a -- basically the excuse for putting up roadblocks and denying access to journalist, 1992, 1993, even 1994 we could get about quite easily. I was able when based in -- in Vitez in 1993 to go through Sierra 1, the most notorious roadblock above Ilidza. And I could go to Grbavica and see my friend there and report on the situation and get back. By 1995 the ABiH was imposing great movement restrictions. I was unable to get to the -- to fighting going on roundabout Tuzla which I wanted to do. We were unable directly to cover the fall of Glamoc and Grahovo, which were tipping points in the war. So 1995 was a very frustrating time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again just for those that might not be familiar with geography or the makeup of the fall of Glamoc and Grahovo, where were those villages located and what ethnicity predominated?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are -- those townships, really, were up against the Croatian border and they were liberated, taken, use whatever words you wish, by Croatian main force units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to revisit the issue of some of your sources. One of the sources that you have named in your prior statements is of some interest to us in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would therefore like to call up 1D656 at this time, which again will be the February 1996 statement that we looked at previously, given to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, and I would like to take a look at page 11 of the same in English and page 12 of the B/C/S translation. And I want to focus on, I believe, the fifth paragraph from the top of the page in the English version, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to read this portion to you and then I will have some follow-up questions for you, sir. "I did Mostar mostly from the Croat side. It was so dangerous. A good source for me was Jusuf Brezina nicknamed 'Yuka.' He had been a small time hoodlum in Sarajevo before the war. He was an effective defender of the city when the fighting began in April/May. When the Bosnian army formed, he took off with his men to Mount Igman where they set up their own base in a ski hotel. The Serbs came looking for him and killed his second in command. He defected to the Croats and fought for them and with them. In May 1993, he and 100 of his men were living in block of JNA barracks in Mostar. Jeremy Bowen did the Muslim side. Bowen is now a corespondent in Jerusalem. I was so close to the battle in Mostar. I don't know who was running the war. I was moving where my access was, and it was with Yuka." And first of all, sir, I have to ask, this selection from your statement, do you stand by the same today as being truthful and accurate and would you repeat the same testimony if asked to do so under the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now as a matter of clarification, the Jusuf Brezina with a B who is mentioned here, is this actually an individual Juka Prazina, P-r-a-z-i-n-a, an ethnic Bosnian Muslim who had been commander of an ABiH unit in Sarajevo and indeed who had been a criminal before the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- what can I tell you? I always spelt his name with a B but we called him Yuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
