utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And when you say that you moved with Yuka, I take that to mean in Mostar, did you have contact with him whilst he was operating in the Sarajevo municipality as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Things were so confused and moving so rapidly. I met him -- first one of my cameraman, a Croat knew him well, and made the introduction. And one of the -- the first time I remember meeting him, he had a rocket-propelled grenade on his shoulder on a street corner in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of becoming familiar with this gentleman and spending time with him, did he become quite candid about his activities that he had undertaken while in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this distance asking him what happened in -- in -- in Sarajevo. I -- I heard -- I believe that he was -- that Haris Silajdzic was one of those who -- who wanted to get rid of the, shall I -- shall we call them the freelance entrepreneurs on the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record at this time when he was in Mostar, he was actually with the HVO, that is the Croat forces, and was indeed now fighting against the Bosnian Muslims forces; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in fact, he had engaged in fighting or combat with his own force, that is the Bosnian Muslims forces, whilst in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that he'd been fighting certainly alongside the Bosnian Muslim forces. Yes. He was found dead in a ditch in Belgium some years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to move on. We received an information report from the Prosecution late on Wednesday, that is the 30th of January, and it identified that you had stated that you were never directly experiencing any Mujahedin but you recall one incident in September 1995 involving beheadings. Could you please tell us if this information we received is correct, and if you can any more details about these beheadings involving Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included this information -- the book I wrote, I wrote entirely in the course of the war, and at the time I wrote it this incident had not happened. It -- it is indisputable that it did happen. I've included it in my new introduction to the -- to the new edition. And my friends in Belgrade tell me one of the reasons that the Serbs had difficulty in dealing with the political aftermath of the Srebrenica massacre was, they said, "Look what happened to our people in this place in September 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take that, sir, that the incident, of which I only had the information that I have given, related to Serbian victims of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were Serbian -- Bosnian Serb soldiers who had surrendered in the course of a battle and were held and then executed. And there had been nothing of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to -- I guess the statement that we have up on the screen, if we could turn to the 12th page in English and the 13th page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber now receives information which is new is not -- Could we ask you to get an impression of the incident you describe, how many people were killed after they had surrendered? How many Bosnian Serb soldiers were killed? Could you give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am told it was in the order of about 50, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was it established to whom they had surrendered and who had killed them as far as you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- it was later established, Your Honour, but certainly at the time I was still -- my book was about to be published and I only actually heard about it much later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what did you hear about the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they were the Mujahedin in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia. Any further details as to the location or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it in the -- on my computer and in my book, Your Honour, but not in my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists the Chamber, these matters were the subject of the Delic case before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then at least not to say that we have now full information about the incident you have added, but at least we have a very rough impression now. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again I believe we are looking at the 12th page in English and the 13th page in B/C/S of this statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, sir. And I'd like to focus on the second half of the page in English, and the paragraphs -- there are two paragraphs there that relate to some additional information relating to the Mujahedin that I would like to ask you about. You say here: "On January 14 I went to Lasva Valley. It was a case where some Croats had lost some trench lines and took them back. They had killed some Mujahedin. I don't think it had any political significance. "On January 29th, an aid worker named Paul Godal was killed by some out of control Mujahedin." Can you first of all verify that these two paragraphs are truthful and accurate and that you would stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed, I stand by this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now then -- you also mentioned Mujahedin earlier in reference to one of my earlier questions. The question I have for you now is: Did you have information that the Bosnian Muslim president, Alija Izetbegovic, had been involved in the formation of an all-Mujahedin unit near Sarajevo that was several thousand strong?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always my understanding, Mr. Ivetic, that the -- that the foreign fighters operated alongside the ABiH but not under their commander and control. But this information -- your information may be correct. I just don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about what you did know. Would you agree -- or could you agree that the Mujahedin were a feature in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, that they were present and active from the beginning of the war and for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe they were active at the beginning of the war. But then those pictures of broken mosques and fallen minarets and tens of thousands of fleeing Muslims, they had a big impact in the Arab and Islamic world who responded with sending aid. I once flew into Sarajevo on the floor of a Saudi aircraft. But come about the later months of 1992 and early 1993, foreign fighters started to infiltrate into Central Bosnia and they -- they set up a base there. They were very intimidating to the press and indeed to the -- the aid workers. The reason we know about this, Paul Godal being killed, was two of the aid convoy drivers, both British, were captured and they ran away and they managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that testimony, sir. I would now like to focus again -- focus your attention to the moment you arrived at Sarajevo, and I would like to try to get an idea of the situation that prevailed at the time. And at paragraph 19 of your amalgamated statement or consolidated statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have P832 MFI, and it will be page 6 in both the B/C/S and the English versions the same so that people can follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You -- well, I'll wait for it to come up. I apologise. At this paragraph you talk about how when you arrived in Sarajevo in March of 1992 and how the ethnic parties had been established and that no non-ethnic parties had a chance, can I get you to confirm that here what you are talking about would be the ethnic political parties that were divided amongst the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs, and the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Ivetic. That is true. I would only amplify that by saying at the time there was a huge peace movement of local citizens trying to head off the war that they saw coming, and they had a peace march one of those days in early March, a demonstration, which was shot at. And it was at that time that the first fatal casualty of the war occurred, who was actually a Serb shot at a wedding party. And we attended his funeral in the official cemetery which later became part of the front line. And we wondered how many more. How many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You raised two points. I'll deal with the last one first. You say that the first fatal casualty of the war was a Serb shot at a wedding party. Did you have any information as to the source of the fire that had killed that Serb at the wedding party?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had, I have forgotten it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to discuss the first part of your answer which dealt with a peace movement of local citizens, and I would direct your attention to paragraph 21, at the bottom of the page in the English of this statement, and it bleeds over to the next page. And I believe here you are talking about a demonstration that was fired upon in April of 1992. Is this the same incident that you have just identified, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a different demonstration. This one was a demonstration of -- of -- of miners, among other people. I -- outside the parliament building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You identify here in the statement, you say this was a big peace demonstration in Sarajevo of Yugoslavs. Would you agree with me that this would indicate that the participants of this march were precisely the non-ethnic political groups that were opposed to the three ethnic political parties that we mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they saw themselves as Yugoslavs in the Tito'st tradition. But of course these demonstrations did not last very long as the descent into war was so rapid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that during this time-period in Sarajevo, that is March, April, and even May of 1992, the situation is quite chaotic, tense, and unpredictable?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a good definition of it -- a description.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to take a moment to view a video together with you relating to some comments that a Mr. Colm Doyle made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For these purposes, Your Honours, I will be playing the video twice, per the standing procedure that we have in the courtroom, so that the audio can be checked with the booths. I have given the transcripts that we have that were disclosed to us to the booths, and I have the video queued.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so, sir, I will be playing it twice, and then after the second time I will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, since we are playing a video now and this is not in relation to you playing the video, but the French interpreters have expressed concerns about the speed of speech not being provided with the proper information. And I noticed that we have no French translation on the record of the words spoken in those videos. We also received information that the new procedure with the -- with CLSS means that we still have to wait quite a while before it has been verified. Now, the whole new procedure was meant to save time in court. At this moment it seems that it causes more problems than it saves time. I just want to put this on the record, and also for the French interpreters, for the French booth, to let them know that we'll pay appropriate attention to the problems they have expressed. But this was just because we are playing a video, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed with playing the video twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps I can also assist the booths. The videos that I have prepared -- the transcripts -- are snippets from the entireties of the videos, and so the transcript that is provided is all in its entirety, the selection that we are showing, so there should not be a need to search through the transcript for the appropriate part. I have tried to compartmentalise it so that from beginning to end is the entirety of the selection that is being shown. So I hope that assists the booths.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, to interrupt. I didn't catch, first of all, the 65 ter number. And can counsel just confirm to me that the transcripts are the same transcripts that were in e-court last night in relation to the videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were printed from e-court this morning and distributed to the booths with the assistance of the usher. And it's 1D632 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "What I'm saying is there are paramilitary people in the city who are under nobody's control and they come from all ethnic backgrounds. And they have to come under someone's control because they, together with others, are destroying the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, I will now play it the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "What I'm saying is there are paramilitary people in the city who are under nobody's control and they come from all ethnic backgrounds. And they have to come under someone's control because they, together with others, are destroying the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, having viewed this video with us, I would ask: Do you remember having a role in making this video?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interviewed Colm Doyle on a number of occasions, but I don't -- this could have been my interview but I have no recollection of it having been so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, based on the times that you interviewed Mr. Colm Doyle, that he expressed sentiments either identical to or similar to what we have seen in this video?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed, Mr. Ivetic. He was a -- he started off as a European Community monitor and he became Lord Carrington's representative. So he was the -- for this time he was representing the international community on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of his reference to the city, would you -- do you have an understanding of that to be Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take that to be Sarajevo, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based on the knowledge and experiences that you had at the time, would you agree with Mr. Doyle's comments as being accurate or would you disagree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time -- I'd like to know the date of that, sir. Do we have a date for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if we ... unfortunately not, sir, all I have is that it is from the original video V000-0799, which to me or to you does not give a date, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I might be able to assist, Your Honour. This is a portion of a full report that starts at 48:05 and runs to 50:15, and I think if the entire report were presented it would make clear what the time-period is. It would ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the parties could agree on that, it would be appreciated. The witness is now unaware. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I guess at this time could I also tender the video and the transcript as the next available Defence number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Actually, I do object. The witness actually couldn't remember this interview and, in my respectful submission, he's been presented with five seconds of an interview with no context, no date. I have no objection if my friend wants to put in the entire two- or three-minute interview with the appropriate transcripts, but otherwise there is no context at all for the Trial Chamber or for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the questions have been asked to the witness as to the video, he has identified that the -- the situation that he saw -- that he agreed with the comments made by Mr. Doyle, so it has evidentiary value. I don't believe that I have to show entire videos in court and use up my time doing so, nor do I have transcripts necessarily of all videos. And so I think that for the purpose of the testimony that this witness has given, this video has meaning. It -- I haven't shown him the rest of the report. It might be something that the Prosecution wants to bring up in redirect. They have a right to do so. But for purposes of the questions that I posed to the witness, this video I think suffices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wants the video to be MFI'd, would like to be informed about context and about date, and we'll then finally decide on admission. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D632 receives number D166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can return back to the e-court. I think we still have your statement up there. Yes. If we can return to paragraph 21 of your statement. Here you had at that time said that you believed that the shots came from Karadzic's people upon this peace movement. Would you agree that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we scroll to paragraph 2. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe the statement as to Karadzic's people is on page 7 in e-court of the English. I'll wait for that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say here that you believe that the shots came from the direction of the Holiday Inn where you noted Karadzic had an office. Would you agree that we cannot with any degree of certainty identify the actual shooters, given the situation on the ground and the presence of various ethnic-paramilitaries out with anyone's control?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, this is why I phrased that as I did. The crowd believed that it had been shot at by Karadzic's people, which is why it storm the Holiday Inn. I don't think it was ever established who actually fired the shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes -- oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. Yes. No, I'm five minutes too early, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right then. If we can turn to 1D654. Hopefully I can get this in within the five minutes. This is the Karadzic transcript of the 14th December, 2010; and if we can look at page 67 of this document in e-court, which should be transcript page 9820. And I would focus on line 17 through 24 to present the witness with this selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could follow along, I will read to you: "Q. Do you agree that from the very outset, there were numerous groups, Muslim groups, that were armed and that were in town? "A. There were certainly armed Muslim groups, and there were armed Serb groups which appeared to me in many cases to be completely ad hoc, so they had improvised. "Q. Thank you. Do you agree that at first the JNA was expected to be between the two parties and prevent the conflict? "A. That was my understanding at the very beginning, yes." Sir, can you confirm for us whether this selection from the transcript that I have read -- do you stand by the same as being truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, now, when Mr. Karadzic refers to "in town," are you and he both talking about the town of Sarajevo in this selection?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the city of Sarajevo. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could help us out, what time-period are you talking about in this selection?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about the -- the -- the early period while Sarajevo was descending into war. I remember there was a proposal at the -- at this time, one of many proposals to bring peace and talk this down, for joint JNA Muslim and Serb patrols but nothing ever came of it. But at this stage the JNA was certainly seen as a potential mediator and a force to come between -- possibly to come between the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the purpose of trying to tie it down, would you agree that this would have been sometime in 1992, perhaps before April or --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm talking about here, sir, is during the early days of April after the peace demonstration was shot at. Or remembering that I, myself, didn't reach Sarajevo till about the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we are now at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before the break, this is the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. Would you please follow the usher, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Since we are waiting for the witness, Mr. Groome, the dubious role of Juka Prazina in Sarajevo, is that an issue which is in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would need some time to examine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am happy to do that over the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, what I'm doing, I'm explore to what extent we hear evidence which is on matters which are in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again, Your Honour, the Prosecution's position is that we are always willing to do that. We just want to be cautious about making commitments or agreeing to facts that might not be reliable off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, one of the issues here is that if the Defence elicits evidence which is in support of its own case that there, of course, is not much notice. And if that takes up to 60 or 70 per cent of the -- of the examination, then it may cause some practical problems as far as court management is concerned. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to take a look at another aspect of this same transcript that we still have up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have the 57th page of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 9810 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then if you'll please bear with me, sir, I want to walk you through two questions and two answers that you gave from lines 18 onwards, and it will transfer on to lines 1 through 5 of the following page as well once we get to there. So I'd like to begin: "Q. At that time, we met, you and I, in the Serbian part of Ilidza. Do you remember that we both had offices in the same hotel and held press conferences there? "A. Yes, indeed, I remember it vividly. "Q. Thank you. Do you recall one attack by Muslim Green Berets who fired even at your hotel where you were staying, although they were not targeting you deliberately, but they were firing at the Serbian part of Ilidza? I believe that was in April of 1992? "A. Yes. I remember that attack vividly. In fact, I had a bullet pass very close to my head and bury itself in the wall behind me which I dug out and put in my pocket as a -- as a sort of a good luck mascot. And a friend of mine, an agency cameraman, was quite badly wounded in that attack." And, sir, first of all, can you confirm the truthful -- truthfulness and accuracy of the statement that I have just read and if you stand by the same today?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And both -- well, Mr. Karadzic refers to Muslim Green Berets and you do not -- you seem to understand what he's referring to. For everyone else and for the record, could you verify whether in fact we are talking about the Bosnian government forces loyal to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, or are we talking about some ethnic-paramilitary at this time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular battle which lasted for most of the day I think occurred on the 2nd of April, 1992, and in the course of these things you can't identify what -- what the actual name or badge of the unit is firing on you, but the firing was certainly coming from the government held side of the lines, yes. And the cameraman was very badly wounded in the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yesterday during your direct examination you at one point had mentioned that you were, I believe, bombed out of your hotel at some point in time. And I'd like to ask you, sir, in fact the bombs, or the grenades, or whatever they were, the shells that were coming that forced you to leave your hotel, were those also coming from the government held side of the lines?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a little bit more complex than that, Mr. Ivetic. I handed over the whole operation to another BBC correspondent about the 7th of -- of May, and in the -- one of the days following that, the hotel in Ilidza was subject to a mortar attack which one of the mortars actually exploded in the -- in the BBC office or near it. The editing equipment was damaged, and they took the collective decision to leave immediately. There was a great press convoy that went out to -- to -- to Split. And, of course, I wasn't -- I wasn't there then, but I was then the one who had to come back in across the airport runway in the middle of June. So I wasn't particularly grateful to my predecessor for this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to now play another video. And this one will be 65 ter 1D629. And again, Your Honours, I would follow the same procedure with the playing of the video twice, and the transcript, I believe, for the whole video from beginning to end is distributed to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, may I ask a few additional questions in order to better understand the basis of your knowledge. You said in as far as the incident where your bullet hit you when you were at the hotel, were you in the hotel? Were you outside of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was standing on a balcony of the hotel doing a live broadcast to London for the morning news, and we came -- it didn't hit me, but I could almost -- there is a certain -- you can -- you can hear the sound of it and it hit the wall behind me. And I just -- I said, I'm sorry, we've got to bring this to an end. It is endangering the lives of the people with me. So that was the end of the broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that hotel was approximately at what distance from the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite close. I would think that the confrontation line would be around 200, 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that made you conclude that the shot was fired from the other side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I took it rather personally, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine. Thank you for that information. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Playing the video the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "The Serbs here are on the defensives, but holding the line. The front line ... to the west of the city, in the area of ... city heartland which had been the secure headquarters both of the European Community observers and of the foreign press. A morning cold ... barrel of the gun. Many guns on both sides. This is a mainly Serbian enclave. And it seems that the Muslims ... withe their relative success in the city centre late yesterday ... they were met with stuff resistance by the Serbs. Into the battle of fire and movement in which the Serbs were trying to improve their positions three by three, across the parkland. It was also dangerous obviously for the photographers. The veteran VIZ news cameraman Rob ... who shot these pictures is the ... forward and paid penalty for it. He was taken to an army hospital and then turned to Belgrade where he is now safe. It was up to this point the federal army's only involvement into the battle. "An 11.00 a.m. ceasefire deadline came and went and the flighting after it was, if anything, fiercer than it was before. There is no mediation. There are no peace talks. Only Serbs and Muslims battling it out ... peacemakers were here on the spot, a dangerous one. They included the personal envoy of Lord Carrington who was due to visit tomorrow. "We have to consider whether or not at this stage of this important visit ... "Or if the will for peace is here. "We don't know whether it is at the moment. We've made a lot of appeals. The situation is very serious. We are not too sure what we are going to do at this stage. "The battle lasted for a full ten hours. Only then did it begin to subside. The Serbs had held their positions, but at a cost which both sides are still counting. One of the Serbian soldiers told me how three of his comrades fell fighting alongside him. "My cousin, two my cousins, and one my best friend. I don't know what talk about, but it was very bad."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, Your Honours, the second playing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The Serbs here are on the defensives, but holding the line. The front line ... to the west of the city, in the area of ... city heartland which had been the secure headquarters both of the European Community observers and of the foreign press. A morning cold ... barrel of the gun. Many guns on both sides. This is a mainly Serbian enclave. And it seems that the Muslims ... withe their relative success in the city centre late yesterday ... they were met with stuff resistance by the Serbs ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop. I receive a message from the French booth that the transcript is not complete and that it goes too quick for simultaneous translation. Therefore, Mr. Ivetic, could you try to find out as soon as possible or by any of the other team members where apparently an incompleteness of the transcript has been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could inquire, I do know that when I handed them out there was some that were doubled sided. Is it perhaps that the second part is on the other page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now the French channel again, Mr. Ivetic does not exclude for the possibility that the transcripts being handed out are double sided?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The transcript is incomplete in the sense that there are some sentences missing on the one-sided page that we have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is apparently that sentences are missing, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is possible, Your Honours. These are the -- it is my understanding these were the transcripts that were used in the Karadzic case, but I obviously have no way of, at this stage, correcting any deficiencies apart from having the video submitted for transcription, I guess, by CLSS at the conclusion of its use in court. I am at Your Honour's indulgence as to how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I would do -- of course, you should verify, if it comes from another case, whether it's accurate, yes or no. I mean, that's our daily job here in this courtroom, to see whether the material is accurate. We cannot proceed like this unless -- if you don't need to rely on the text, then the witness at least has seen the video. So if there are any questions you would put to him without relying on the text, then we could perhaps at a later stage see whether -- whether we could use the text by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could proceed that way, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, with respect to this particular clip, do you confirm that it is a piece that you had a role in preparing or providing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was my reporting for the BBC. It was dated the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this the incident that we had just discussed from the Karadzic transcript wherein your friend and agency cameraman was quiet badly wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does it accurately depict the scene as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now am I correct that the only involvement of the JNA was in assisting in the urgent evacuation of the wounded cameraman and that the JNA did not take part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the JNA had already been planning to withdraw but it had been repeatedly attacked by the armed Bosnian Muslim forces in the days prior to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, the -- the JNA was -- was planning to withdraw, but it was encircled in the -- the barracks which were General Kukanjac's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it your information and recollection at the time that both the Serbs and Muslim sides were well armed for purposes of this battle?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the -- as far as I can judge and I could judge at the time, the -- both sides were using small arms and mortars in the -- in the battle for this hotel in Ilidza. And as for the barracks when I went there, before the pullout they showed me some of the shell fragments, the mortars that had landed in their compound. In fact, they had them all laid out on a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I guess at this time I should probably ask for the video to be MFI'd pending the procedure that we discussed and before I move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wouldn't object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D629 receives number D167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would like to take a look at another clip with you, and hopefully with the first read-through we'll hear feedback from the booths as to whether the transcript is sufficient or not. And in case it isn't, I would ask you at least follow along with the first viewing, sir, so if we have to rely upon just asking questions on the scenes that we may do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will change at the end of the first round of playing this video, I'll move to the French channel and see whether there are any comments. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: There has been a gun battle going on around this hotel" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we please have the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is number 1D631.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we restart it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: There has been a gun battle going on around this hotel in the parkland all morning ... it is quite intense. We have now been told and rather the European Community monitors have been warned that this place has been targeted for incoming mortar fire some time around now. So it's not a very comfortable situation ... that is a hard one to say ... the -- the -- I'm sorry, it's a little bit disturbing, some of this noise. The Muslims are in a very difficult position geographically. The Serbs have ... and the Serbs and army have them surrounded. On the other hand, the Muslims fought back strongly yesterday, and as far as I can tell what's going on here is ... match."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before proceeding with the second playing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now move to the French channel. I again received a message that the transcript is not complete, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May we then have it marked for identification and I'll ask the witness questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis -- Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I have a further concern with this video, which is similar to a previous issue which is again this is an excerpt of a report and the context, I think, is -- or some of what is being shown is qualified. If the full report is played, there is additional information the Prosecution would want to rely on. And I'm trying to avoid the situation of having to play that in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually if an excerpt of a book or a video or whatever is played or shown to the Chamber, the other party is always entitled to ask for -- for context and adding portions, yes or no. I do not know whether the entirety of this video is available to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have the entire clip located, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can have a look at it. You can ask if you think that this distorts what the clip really is about, then you can, of course at a later stage, you can try to have that added. Now if that's impossible today, we'll have to see whether it's -- the context which makes sense to give without the witness or whether we would have to recall the witness for that, and we'll then see how matters develop. At this time it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this may serve as guidance for the Prosecution and for the Defence in similar circumstances. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D631 receives number D168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, having seen the video portion, can you identify just by having looked at the pictures when this one would have been prepared and if it was prepared by -- obviously by someone affiliated with your office?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's the same battle, the beginning of it, and the date is the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this the time-period -- strike that. And does this appear to be an authentic clip from your report that you were preparing for the BBC at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was what we call a live two-way into their -- into their morning news. The reason the cameraman weaves about and take pictures of everybody else is there was a -- the European Broadcasting Union was co-ordinating all our reports at that time and they wanted to make some publicly for themselves about how they were performing under fire, so there was a second camera taking wider pictures of the same, but the BBC camera was on me there. It was a straight-forward two-way interview for the BBC morning news, and what you played earlier was a report assembled at the end of the ten hours fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one additional question. We saw a white building in the background. Was that still on the same side of the confrontation line you were, or was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building you saw, Your Honour, was another part of the same hotel complex. There was a Hotel Serbia and Hotel Bosnia, all part of the same hotel complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the confrontation line was, looking at the video, left, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking -- it was to the right of the hotel where the cameraman got wounded because the fire was coming from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now move to other matters you have personal knowledge of. And I'd like to turn back to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can have P832 MFI in e-court. And I will be looking at paragraph 65, which is on page 18 of the English and page 19 of the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now here you are discussing an incident from the 2nd of May, 1992, when the elements of the Bosnian government side attacked the JNA officers' club. And you say here: "They did not wish to be observed by the press."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sixty-five. I apologise. The quote is in the middle of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want to ask you, first of all, with relation to this incident, do you know if there were casualties on the JNA side arising from the same?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I was -- I was -- we were intimidated out of it -- out of this -- what's called a Dom Armija, and we were shown very clearly at gunpoint that our -- this is by Muslim government backed militia, that our presence was not welcome. And then we retreated to the main street and it was a heavy battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I want to focus on this intimidation or this -- how you describe it, that they did not wish to be observed by the press. Did this type of treatment and position persist even later in the war; that is, that the Bosnian Muslim side did not wish its activities to be reported by the press?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it unusual to have been threatened in quite this way, a bloke pointing his gun at you. There were other cases later in the war. There was one where a Serb family was evicted from a block of high-rise apartments near the television station and a cameraman went to try and find out what was happening -- a photographer, rather, and he got all his tyres shot at. It was unusual but it did happen occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to revisit the Karadzic transcript at this time from the 15th of September, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D655 in e-court. And if we could turn to page 9 of this document in e-court. That should be transcript page 9863 of the Karadzic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would focus on line 16 through 23 of that page. And if you could follow along, sir, I'll have some questions for you after I read this into the record: "Q. Actually, we establish here, Mr. Bell, that the Muslims concealed their weaponry from the UN rather skillfully. Did they allow you access to their heavy weapons in town? Were you aware of the deployment of their heavy weapons in town? "A. I was aware that they had at least one tank in a tunnel. Occasionally, we would come across their mortar positions, and it became a very sensitive issue with their field security, so that if we showed their mortars firing, we might suffer the consequences." And first, sir, can I ask you if you can confirm if you stand by this testimony from the Karadzic proceedings as being truthful and accurate today having taken the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that this would relate to a time-period much later than May of 1992? Could you assist us about that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly -- the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina became much more -- much more like a regular army as the time passed, and this included a tightening of its field security. And the people we were dealing with were worried that if we showed their mortars firing; for instance, there was one mortar position on the low ground just to the east of the Turkish fort, and we had a big debate among ourselves whether we should use it or whether we'd be retaliated against and our movements restricted. And I think probably we decided to play safe. But this was a development much later in the war, at the time when our access was being limited in a way. I would also add that they were, of course, the -- the government forces were outgunned in heavy weapons from the start to the finish of the siege. They didn't have that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and when you say "you might suffer the consequences," what kind of consequences could you expect? Was anything ever threatened or made known to you about the result of any action to show their positions or their use of heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember a time when -- when Sky News ran some footage of mortars being fired from a position about half a mile from the television station, and the authorities got very upset about it and were -- were certainly threatening to withdraw Sky News accreditation. But we were -- we were all under -- you know, in a sense you're -- you're the guests of the -- of the -- of the authorities on the side out of which you -- we -- out of which you operate, and it was a particularly difficult time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question: Did they finally withdraw the Sky News accreditation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they do not, sir. No they did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I now want to now return again to your statement briefly, P873 MFI, and paragraphs 66 of the same which again will be on page 18 in the English version and page 19 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, I can let you know that the part of the paragraph that I am talking about deals with the ambush of the JNA convoy by the Bosnian Muslim forces. And can you first of all clarify for us that this is in fact the incident that you mentioned earlier in cross-examination where you had contacted your editors and told them what happened and they had asked are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is indeed that same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a little more detail about this incident in terms of was this convoy, in fact, part of a planned and previously agreed withdrawal of the JNA in compliance with the United Nations resolutions that the JNA withdraw to the new boundaries of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly a -- a limited exchange that had been agreed between General Kukanjac, who had to get out of the city, and Alija Izetbegovic who had been kidnapped by the Serbs the night before with his daughter on his return from -- from Lisbon, and this was negotiated locally by the United Nations and it went wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I have a video. And again, Your Honour, I would suggest that we play it through once and see if we have the same issues with the translations -- or, excuse me, the transcripts. If we do, then I would follow the same procedure that we use for the first couple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way to find out whether the matters you want to deal with is -- are in dispute, or? I mean, your last question was whether it was announced, I think, compliance that -- whether it was a planned and previously agreed withdrawal. Is there any dispute about that, Ms. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, we heard evidence on that from Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which does not mean that there is no dispute. Sometimes you hear evidence where you still dispute. But I do understand that it's not in dispute. That, Mr. Ivetic, again, let's try to elicit evidence from this witness on matters which are in dispute. But let's play the video --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what number is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have listed 1D633.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it for the first time. And Ms. Bolton, if you will please be very alert on matters where you say the Prosecution agrees with what it sees or what it asked of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "This army is staying in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he said. We are withdrawing from certain areas, especially those most under attack, but we will continue to be the army of the people who shelter and accept us. Outside of the room where he was talking, the evidence of the most recent attack. His headquarters at the old part of town was shot at again last night. This is an angry general. Mortars, rockets, snipers, bazookas, heavy machine-guns, he listed the weapons used against the headquarters and produced the evidence. What he called his souvenirs along with the warning against whoever might try it again. "If we are attacked we shall retaliate fiercely. "He ... was a declaration of war by the Croats and Muslims led by President Alija Izetbegovic. The army until now has been more neutral in this war than it was in Croatia but its patience is strained. It was moving today to the Serbian side of the lines and taking its big guns with it. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'll first move again to the French channel to see whether they have complete transcript. There is a complete transcript available. So you may play it for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I just want to note that the transcript that's provided actually continues for several paragraphs, and I would just ask that perhaps when they are filed we file one separate transcript for each segment on -- that's played, because right now you might read it and think that this is all one continuous conversation and it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that what will be tendered is exclusively the portions that were played, but we'll see it at the very end whether it's covers all of it, yes or no. At this moment, Mr. Ivetic, may play for a second time, and we'll have French translation of the audio. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. And I can also -- I guess for the record we have stopped at 1 minute and 7 seconds of this video. There is material afterwards. I was hoping to not spend time if we had a bad translation to view the whole thing but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "This army is staying in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he said. We are withdrawing from certain areas, especially those most under attack, but we will continue to be the army of the people who shelter and accept us. Outside of the room where he was talking, the evidence of the most recent attack. His headquarters at the old part of town was shot at again last night. This is an angry general. Mortars, rockets, snipers, bazookas, heavy machine-guns, he listed the weapons used against the headquarters and produced the evidence. What he called his souvenirs along with the warning against whoever might try it again. "If we are attacked we shall retaliate fiercely. "He ... was a declaration of war by the Croats and Muslims led by President Alija Izetbegovic. The army until now has been more neutral in this war than it was in Croatia but its patience is strained. It was moving today to the Serbian side of the lines and taking its big guns with it. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, this clip that we have seen, can you confirm the authenticity of the clip? Is it one that you had a role in producing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first of all, the gentleman that was at the beginning of the clip in the military uniform, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with which armed force was he affiliated?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he was a general in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And he recounted attacks by various weapons, including mortars, bazookas, heavy machine-guns, et cetera, was it your recollection that he also mentioned anything about casualties that had been endured by his forces as part of that attack by the opposing force?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not mention casualties which suggested to me that there had not been any because he certainly would have mentioned casualties if there had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it your understanding at this point in time that the JNA had restrained itself and had not returned fire upon those who had fired upon it; that is to say, the Bosnian forces that were attacking?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case at the time, Mr. Ivetic. We are talking about the very early days in May 1992, but [indiscernible] the situation did change.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by that time, the very early days in May 1992, is it accurate based upon your knowledge of information that the -- that the Bosnian Muslim side had for several days attacked this JNA headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the -- the evidence is -- is undeniable. Now, whether you'd classify these as heavy weapons, I don't think that they were. Not in the usual definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to the ambush that you discuss in your statement, which I believe is paragraph 66, on the 3rd of May, did you have information at that time that around the same date there were other such incidents throughout the remainder of Bosnia-Herzegovina where JNA convoys or JNA positions were ambushed or attacked by Bosnian government or Bosnian Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ivetic, that all I knew at that time was -- was what I reported there, because the communications across Bosnia were beginning to break down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could have this first clip going from 0 to 1 minute and 7 seconds of 1D633 marked for identification pending, I guess, uploading a transcript that is limited to it and providing perhaps even an excerpt that is limited to just the portion that we viewed and which the witness has testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D633 receives number D169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to return to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we could please have up in e-court P873, MFI. And I'd like to look at paragraphs 23 through 41. So if we could first start off on page 7 in English and page 7 in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, according to my notes, paragraphs 23 through 41, which covers pages 7 through 9 of your statement in both languages, relate to the evidence as to Zvornik and to Arkan and his forces. In any event, this particular set of events, am I correct that all of these events relating to Zvornik, to Bijeljina, and to Arkan in respect to these two places all date from April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was an eviction of Muslims from Bijeljina later in the war, but this is very specifically actually more about -- about Zvornik than Bijeljina and the -- and the territory in land where the Bosnian Muslims were fleeing from their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to these events that were recounted at these paragraphs of your statement, again paragraphs 23 through 41, I believe you have the hard copy and can leaf through them to see which ones I am talking about. But I'd like to find out with respect to these specific incidents of which you have in your direct examination and in your statement provided evidence, if these are limited to April of 1992 as far as Zvornik is concerned with the caveat that you do mention seeing Arkan in 1994 in Serbia. But that the events in Zvornik are all April of 1992. If you can --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly down to paragraph 31. It is about these particular places and about Arkan himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir. And would you agree that that is all April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps -- and likewise, you have some discussions there of meetings or encounters with Arkan that deal with 1991. For instance, seeing him in Erdut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I became aware of him as -- as a force in the Croatian civil war when my colleagues from French television came in with some quite remarkable footage of the Serb's capture of a village called Laslovo. So I then went to see him in Erdut and I go to know him really well, and I -- sometimes I would visit him in the ice-cream parlor that he ran near the gates of Red Star football -- football club, and he even offered me membership of Red Star football club. I -- I -- I used him for -- because he was -- he was doing things, and access is everything in war reporting, and if you only dealt with people you liked you wouldn't get very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood, sir. Now with respect to this time-period when you were meeting with Arkan in 1991, when you were reporting upon -- reporting about events in Zvornik and Bijeljina in 1992, would you agree with me that this was all during the time-period that we previously discussed when there were ethnic paramilitaries of all ethnicities operating at least in Sarajevo, pursuant to the testimony we discussed when we viewed the video from Mr. Doyle. Would you agree that it's all within the same time-period?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all within the same time-period, but Arkan's Tigers, as they were called, were by far the most formidable and best organised of any paramilitary group that I met in either war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, my friend suggested that the time-period that had already been discussed in terms of Sarajevo included 1991, and for the record, in fact, all that's been discussed with respect to Sarajevo is with respect to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we are -- since the flow of evidence is interrupted anyhow, I'd like to deal with a few practical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were supposed to take the next break at 1.00 and then resume at 20 minutes past 1.00, which would leave us another 55 minutes until a quarter past 2.00. First, Mr. Ivetic, could you tell us whether you are on track?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which means, Your Honours, that I have approximately one hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour left. That would mean that first 15 minutes now, then you would need until five minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, as matters stand now, how much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There -- the difficulty I have, Your Honours, with respect to the portions of the videos that I would want to put to the witness, and so I think probably I'm looking at about 20 minutes, 25 minutes right about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that we run over quarter past 2.00. At the same time, we all know that we have a videolink for next Monday. I suggest the following: That we -- and I'm also looking at you, Mr. Lukic, that we extend the last session, although unfortunately I'm unable to sit on from quarter past 2.00, but I do understand that my colleagues are willing to sit under Rule 15 bis for the last perhaps 15 to 20 minutes. Mr. Ivetic, you have got time until five minutes past 2.00. Ms. Bolton will then have another 20 to 25 minutes in an extended session which gives us the expectation that we could finish at 2.30. We'll proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thirty more minutes until the break, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise. Perhaps I can get you back to the frame of thought we had when we were doing the questions. These events in Zvornik and Bijeljina in April of 1992, am I correct that they all predate the arrival of General Mladic to the army of the Bosnian Serbs which was in fact in May of 1990 [sic], if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is beyond my knowledge. I was not aware of exactly when he took command. But, yes, it was in the very early days of the war. And I think the actual date of the Zvornik report was the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 1D656, which is a previous statement that you have given to the Office of the Prosecutor, dated February of 1996. And I'd like to turn to page 5 of the same in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When waiting for it, I just wanted to point out that page 81, line 22, the reference was to May of 1992. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you, Your Honours, for catching that. I'd missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the last paragraph on the page in English, and if you could follow along I would have some questions for you relating to the same after reading into the record. And I begin: "Arkan's troops were not always in theater. He was not seen in the war zones between spring 1992 and autumn 1995. Arkan, I believe, was not welcome as long as Mladic was in control and the front lines were holding. I don't believe he was called to action by anyone in 1995 ..." First of all, sir, can you confirm the accuracy and truthfulness of this part of your 1996 statement and would you so testify here today after having taken the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, that's accurate. But I have one thing to add, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is that I did hear towards the end of the war that Arkan and his men were active in the defence of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that's the continuation of this line. I perhaps should have read to the end. But with that caveat you do accept this to be accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can we take from that, sir, that General Mladic, according to your information, did not tolerate paramilitaries or irregulars and attempted to route them out once he took over the VRS in spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my impression in dealing with the VRS that they were organised as a -- as a professional army. They -- the soldiers admired the accused. They did not wear the -- the emblems of the sort of paramilitaries that we saw, sort of rogue elements, operating in Vukovar, for instance. And if you were -- if you dealt with them a lot, they set great store by what they called correctness. If they called me correct, I knew I was getting along well with them, and they sometimes did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, perhaps for purposes of context, if we can look at your statement, P873, page -- pardon me, P873, MFI'd, and if we can look at paragraphs 113 and 114, at page 29 in English and page 31 in the B/C/S. And again it's page 29 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think you misspoke. The number can't be correct. It is P832.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That is correct. I apologise. P832, MFI'd. And it's page 29 in the English, page 31 in the B/C/S; paragraphs 113 and 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, when those come up, or perhaps in the hard copy if you have it in front of you, the evidence you have just given is in part encapsulated in these paragraphs, and you go into some more detail here where -- at least you compare General Mladic to General Schwarzkopf in 113 and then in 114 you say that: "Under Mladic the army stopped wearing Chetnik symbols and adopted a more organised military style of approach than before." Would you agree with me that these changes instituted by General Mladic didn't happen overnight. It took some time for these changes to take effect, especially to reach the local level units and local level commanders. Was that your experience?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was a reasonable inference, yes, sir. But we were -- you know, we were also hassled and intimidated on a regular basis at road blocks, sort of low level hooliganism. It was not an easy time in which to get about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that during this time-period there was also a severe shortage of mid-level non-commissioned officers within the ranks of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this at the time, but it certainly wouldn't surprise me. You don't create a standing army in a time of war overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we are right about at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you are now five minutes early, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. Then I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to now turn to 1D648, which again will be your book, sir. And I'd like to turn to page 11 in e-court of the same, which, according to my notes, ought to be page 108 of the hard copy of your publication. And it's the middle paragraph on the left side of the screen and I'd like to have you following along, sir, as I read it into the record: "The other thing that I came to understand was that the Serbs' vaunted military superiority was actually quite fragile, and the juggernaut of their army was very far from invincible. They were fully mobilised and permanently overstretched across 800 miles of front line. They had no more resources of manpower to draw on. This was an army which already included all men of military age and some beyond it. On the front lines at Trebevic, overlooking Sarajevo, where the men served two weeks at a time in primitive conditions, it looked like a muster of grandfathers under arms. The Serbs were heavily outnumbered by already rearmed Muslims. They were increasingly vulnerable to infantry attacks, and they were genuinely tired of the war." First of all, sir, this selection that I read from your book, do you stand by these words and would you testify the same way today under the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm actually rather proud of them. I think I got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that at this time most of the other members of the press corps were comitted to a different image of the Serbs as being ruthless warmongers or blood thirsty Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I can answer for other members of the press corps but I can for what I wrote. And if I may just add I discussed this extensively in Pale, socially with Dr. Koljevic, Professor Koljevic, and Jovan Zametica, and I said, Look, if this goes on, you're -- you're going to lose. The Serbs -- the Muslims are getting stronger and you're getting weaker. It can only have one end. And whoever I was talking to he said, We don't aware. That's a strange thing to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apologise. I'm waiting for the transcript. And so we can place this temporally within our greater picture to understand your testimony, am I correct that this testimony relates to the third and fourth years of the war, that would be 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the -- the time of the -- of Operation Storm in Croatia, when the front lines in Bosnia started to change, and I wrote of this extensively, and Dr. Karadzic started wearing a combat uniform jacket, and he was -- he looked -- wanted to look more of a political commander, and we realised then that they had no reserve lines to fall back on because they had never thought that they'd need them, and so they could be rolled up quite quickly which is what happened towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this also the same time-period when General Smith, the head of UNPROFOR, initiated air and artillery strikes against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was all in this time-frame and of course they were all -- they were all connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it your impression that General Smith had somehow changed the rules as far as air-strikes against the Serbs by -- at the behest of UNPROFOR by NATO were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly had -- had -- had the key in his hand. The UN had to turn the key. I think General Janvier was away. But I think the rules were, in fact, changed by the second London conference. And as I've also written, I think the -- the -- when as the evidence of what had happened at Srebrenica began to come to light subsequent to July 1995, that was -- also made a forced or negotiated end game necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, now I believe I am at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are, Mr. Ivetic. Could the witness follow the usher. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, would you agree with me that unfortunately the governments of the policies makers, such as the United States and Great Britain, were largely relying on the media to inform them and bring them up to speed about the Balkans during the time-period of 1992 and 1995 rather than expending their own actions to become more knowledgeable before making decisions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's seven questions in one, Mr. Ivetic. And apart from that, could you please lay a foundation to know exactly what this witness says -- knows about how the governments and the policies makers, that's quite a large group of people, what they did and how they did it and why they did it. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I answer the many-sided question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you can, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best. They had -- the governments had many sources of information. I don't think they were -- they were very favorable to the media reports. I was once described as a founding member of the "Something must be done" club. So I think they had many sources of information, including their own national contingents in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at something from your book, which I think we still have up on the screen. If we could turn to page 22 in e-court, which correlates to page 145 in the text. And I'd like to present this to you, sir, which was the bases for my question. The paragraph is on the second page, that is on the right-hand side, the second paragraph from the bottom. And begins: "The Americans were more candid about it, more open with themselves. Television is an integral and dynamic part of their politics and their culture. They are elected by it and to a large extent they take their decisions by it. CNN's "Newsak" is the mood music of their legislative and executive offices.
