The television sets a great deal of the agenda, said former secretary of state Lawrence Eagleburger, and then the president and his secretary of state have to deal with it. There is just no argument. "I am not suggesting that this is how things should be, only that it is how they are - certainly in America, and more in Britain than our profession pinstripes admit. I don't even welcome the trend. If there is a besetting sin of journalists, especially those of the television variety, it is an overweening sense of our own importance. It is no longer enough for us to be mere reporters, we must be styled as correspondents or even editors - though in my experience a corespondent is no more than a reporter who has lunch. What the world needs probably is not more of us but fewer and humbler. We are certainly not infallible, and it will be easier for everyone when governments inform themselves better. But in Bosnia, they left it to us." Sir, can you confirm whether you stand by the words --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, they are rather colourful, but I stand by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question. You may continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly your words here at the end, that in Bosnia they left it to us, that it was your impression that the British and American decision-makers relied upon the media or were led by the media as to decision-making in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Ivetic, I think the British government regarded me as a bit of a nuisance. They -- there were, of course, other sources of information. There was no British embassy in Washington -- in Sarajevo that were open on a very small scale in 1994 with one diplomat and one spy, I believe. But their sources of information were -- were partly military. British commanders would sometimes -- senior commanders would be summoned to -- to Downing Street. But they didn't like pressure on them coming from people like me to do perhaps more than they were willing to do to try and end this dreadful conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at one other selection from your book at page 108 of this document, which is page 11 in e-court. I apologise. And when the same comes up, it is the selection at the very top of the page on the left, which I'll read for you: "It was not necessary to believe the conspiracy theories about government forces shelling their own people for the benefit of CNN and the BBC, to see that the city's defenders could succeed by failing, they might launch an infantry attack which could make a great commotion and not gain an inch of ground, but yet provoke a fierce retaliation by the Serbs. Small arms would be answered by mortars, and machine-guns by shell fire. And where the shells landed and did their indiscriminate damage, the cameras would never be far away. Nor would the government spokesmen demanding action. This was the way that wars were waged in the age of satellite television and the UN peace enforcement: A military victory could also be a political defeat. The Muslims could win the war by losing it. And vice versa, the Serbs." And, sir, the question I have, is do you stand by these comments that I read from your book as being truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I stand by them absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if we recall at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it comes up again and again, "Do you stand by these comments that I read from your book as being truthful and accurate." Now I'd like to know exactly what was meant by that question and what was meant by your answer. "Truthful," meaning first of all, that you wrote it, I take it. I see that you are nodding yes. Second that you -- where you express opinions and views, that they still are your opinions and views. And "accurate" to be that you never included anything in a false way. Is that -- or is there more? Because if we are talking about accuracy and truthfulness, we usually are focussing on facts. Now I'm not to say that this is not based on the observation of many facts, although they do not appear all here. But is it primarily that you're saying these are still my views and that is how I look at it on the basis of what I know. Is that the gist of your answer or is there anything more, if we are talking about truth and accuracy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an interesting paragraph because it actually is a paragraph of judgements. And I stand by these judgements. Even more now after my experiences of this and other subsequent wars. I think it may be helpful for you to understand. This is the first war I was in in which the means of mass destruction coincided so connectively with the means of mass communication, and that's partly what this paragraph is about. But it's -- yes, I absolutely stand by those judgements. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, you are aware that it's our primary task to deliver the judgements on the matters and that the witnesses are supposed to inform us by giving us their factual knowledge. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to your statement, at paragraph 57 of the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for those following that would be page 16 of both the English and B/C/S of P832, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- you talk about the impression that the -- that was garnered by these actions as to the bombardment of Sarajevo always being constantly unprovoked. Would, in fact, you have any information based on your observations and experiences, if, in fact, the bombardment of Sarajevo was often times or perhaps more often than not provoked by the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where are we exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 57, page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 57, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd say that's hard to judge, Mr. Ivetic. But towards the end of the war, I mean, I've got -- some videos are vivid in my mind, whether or not they are in evidence, of an attempted breakout of the city by the infantry of the ABiH which actually got over the Pale road for a while. And -- but these are -- this is just my cumulated experience over three and a half years of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall that -- first of all, at paragraph 32 of your statement and onwards, you discuss the so-called siege of Sarajevo. I'd like to spend some time briefly going through this. In paragraph 32, which is at page 9 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S of your statement, you describe the situation as a war among the people. And in this regard I want to ask you, did you have knowledge and information available to you at the time that you were in Sarajevo that, in fact, the armed forces of the BiH government were generally billeted in schools and billeted among the general population?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was certainly no -- no barracks for them there. The barracks were largely taken over by UNPROFOR contingents, and therefore they were dispersed among the people to an extraordinary degree. The phrase "war among the people" comes from your previous witness, General Smith, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that as the war progressed, the Bosnian Muslim or BiH forces appeared to be getting more and better weaponry, including anti-tank weapons such as wire-guided anti-tank weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was evidence that some were coming in through Tuzla, but it was very difficult for them to bring heavy weapons into Sarajevo. But they were becoming better armed and this -- these are the points I put to my friends in Pale. They didn't care.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the information report that the Prosecution gave to us a few days ago, it was stated that you never gained access to or used any tunnel in Sarajevo. Can you confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to explore with you another aspect and that would be your knowledge of a tunnel. Did you have knowledge of a tunnel at the Butmir airport being used by the Bosnian Muslims to reinforce and rearm?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the war I did. We were, for obvious reasons of field access, we had no access to it. Our own way into Sarajevo was done -- the logging track into Mount Igman. So the existence of this tunnel -- in television you tend to report things you know for sure and can see and show. And we couldn't get at the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I want to explore with you, again, is something that was mentioned in the Perisic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 1D653. And page 13 of the same in e-court which ought to correlate to transcript page 3177 of the Perisic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would like to focus on lines 3 through 12 of the same. And if you bear with me, sir, I will first read the selection then have some questions for you: "Q. All right. Was there an easy means of entry into and exit from the city for the civilians in ABiH-held territory? "A. There was no easy means at all. There was in the latter half of the war a tunnel constructed underneath the airport runway which provided a means of reinforcement and supplies to come into the city. But for any -- anyone who wanted to leave, unless they had the right permissions and the right influence, I mean, they more or less, they had to endure the whole siege. We were in a different state because we had United Nations passes and we were able with difficulty to come through Bosnian Serb roadblocks in Ilidza and elsewhere." First off, sir, do you stand by this testimony of yours in the Perisic case as being truthful and accurate and would you so testify today the same under the solemn declaration you have taken?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I would also add that of course from August 1994 we could no longer negotiate the Bosnian Serb roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say that people who wanted to leave needed to have the right permissions, am I to take it that this included needing to know the right ABiH personnel who were controlling the ingress and egress through this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The Bosnian authorities controlled the tunnel and absolutely who used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to have knowledge of any allegations of the UN or UNPROFOR personnel being engaged in any black market or other activities in relation to this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in relation to the -- to the tunnel. There were stories told about a black market -- marketeering by the Ukrainian contingent of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since you bring it up, I'd like to go to that, and I'd like to call up 1D648 again. And turn to page 26 of the same in e-court, which will be page 175 of your original version of "In Harm's Way." And here you are talking about an incident involving General Rose. And this would be the second page, that is the right-hand side of the screen. And it will be the approximately fifth or sixth line from the top of the page. And I will read for you, sir, and have some questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, try to do this at such a speed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that the interpreters are able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "His record was that of a tough, no-nonsense soldier who champed at bits and suffered no fools near him. His extra qualification for the UN's Bosnia command was not his knowledge of peacekeeping but his knowledge of French. Having studied for a year at the Sorbonne, he was the only senior British officer with fluent enough French to brief and be briefed in it. "In Sarajevo that mattered, as the encircled city was, in UN terms, a French fiefdom. It had not been intended that way, but the French had replaced the Canadians in July 1992 as part of a tri-national brigade so daft in its conception that only the United Nations ivory tower, its thirty-eighth floor, could have dreamed it up. When the then-UN commander, General Lewis MacKenzie, first told me about it, even he had difficulty believing it. It was known as the 'confessional deployment.' The French were included because they were Roman Catholics, the Egyptians because they were Muslims, and the Ukrainians because they were Orthodox. All it lacked was Copts. The plan was that all the city's constituent peoples would feel in some way spiritually befriended. Of course, it didn't work. And the principal contribution of the Egyptian and Ukrainian battalions was to ease the hardships of those citizens with German marks by selling their food and fuel on the black market. Senior officers tried in vein to express this traffic. When the small Ukrainian contingent in the enclave of Zepa radioed that they had supplies enough only for one more day, their battalion commander was unsympathetic: 'Then tell them that they'll have to buy it back.'" First of all, sir, this selection that I've read for you, I take it that it's based upon information that you had available and perhaps conversations that you had with members of UNPROFOR on the topic. Could you enlighten us on that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could. The language is rather colourful, but the language used to me by some of my friends in UNPROFOR was also colourful. They -- the -- I wasn't going to make much of it because in news reports you don't -- it's a waste of time to criticize UN contingents. But a lot of the British staff officers I knew in UNPROFOR were appalled at what they were seeing. And I was talking to these people every day. They were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can I take it, sir, that the activities that they were appalled by, this black-marketeering was ongoing for a long, extended period, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, my friend has suggest what they were appalled by and the witness has not actually testified to that as of yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. I can ask the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. When I say please do so, I immediately add to that, please do it in such a way that the relevance becoming clear to the Chamber immediately. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say that the British members of the UNPROFOR that you had contact with were appalled by what they were seeing, was that in reference to the back-marketeering on the part of the other contingents? Right here we are talking about the Ukrainian contingent and the Egyptian contingent.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that this had been ongoing for some time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly can't place a time-frame on it, but it was sufficiently conspicuous to -- to offend a lot of professional British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it your experience that such activities led to -- led to increased controls of humanitarian aid convoys that were going into either Sarajevo where the Egyptian contingent was or Zepa where the Ukrainian contingent was? Did you have that kind of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can comment on that at this distance, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct, sir, that at the time that General Rose assumed the command of the UNPROFOR element in Bosnia, that one of his predecessors, General Briquemont, had revealed that some of the national contingents under UNPROFOR had been refusing to take his orders?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not actually in Sarajevo at that time, I was in Central Bosnia. So I'm not sufficiently aware of the circumstances of General Briquemont's departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that there was a time-period when there were some very dire reports coming out of Gorazde that prompted General Rose to undertake and prepare a mission to relieve the pressure on Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember his -- he took no press with him but there was a camera which we used some of the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you detail for us as briefly as possible if, in fact, the dire situations that had been reported by the media that were based primarily I think by reports from purported radio ham operators in Gorazde, whether in fact those dire conditions were verified or if the condition was something different when people actually got into the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was unverifiable. We did a report once based on one of these voices from Gorazde. The closest I was able to get was the high ground with -- over -- overlooking Gorazde. This is when we were still allowed into Bosnian Serbian territory. But the gravity or otherwise of the situation, it was impossible to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that initially General Rose's mission to Gorazde suffered a setback in that the French and the British national authorities had prevented their UNPROFOR contingent troops from following General Rose's orders?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that from time to time the national governments played what was called the -- the yellow or the red card. On this occasion, I wasn't there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about something else in your book, which we still have in front of us. If we could turn to page 29 in actual book -- in the e-court, I apologise. Which is page 181 of the actual book. And the section I want to focus on is the second page which is on the right-hand side. And if you'll bear with me, sir, I would like to present this to you and ask you some questions about it, and then we are near the end of my examination: "His second area of conflict was with NATO, which was by then deployed in its new role as the UN's Bosnian enforcement agency. The Serbs at this time had their tanks already in the outskirts of Gorazde, and the city centre under small-arms fire. They were checked and halted by NATO air-strikes on 10th and 11th April - the first time that the alliance had used such force in its history. The results were mixed. The NATO ground attack aircraft, flying at low level in foul weather, destroyed an elderly tank, some trucks, and a communications centre, at a cost of one British Sea Harrier shot down. In the days that followed they were looking for more targets, while General Rose was urging restraint. He spent an entire day on the telephone to Brussels trying to persuade NATO commanders that the Serbs had halted their advance, it was time to give negotiations a chance, and UNPROFOR was in any case a peacekeeping not a war-fighting force. Also, he was responsible for the safety of his troops, who were endangered by overreaction. In the words of Colonel Simon Shadbolt, General Rose's military assistant, whom some saw as the brain's of the partnership: 'A pre-emptive punitive strike against the Serbs might make people happy over their cornflakes in the morning, but it is not going to help peacekeeping.' Or as the General himself put it, 'Patience, persistens, and pressure is how you conduct a peacekeeping mission. Bombing is a last resort because you then cross the Mogadishu Line.' (M words were much invoked by both sides in the debate on General Rose's stewardship. His defenders praised him for avoiding the errors of Mogadishu. His critics attacked him for repeating the errors of Munich). NATO commanders steeped in the doctrines of overwhelming force, were unimpressed by General Rose's case for restraint - and especially the idea of limited response or 'proportionality' in the selection of targets for air-strikes. 'Proportionality' explained one of them, 'I'll give you proportionality. Han Pijesak (headquarters of the Bosnian Serb army) and Pale ammunition dump and Lukavica barracks. That's proportionality).'" First of all, sir, do you stand by these words from your book as being accurate, and do you stand by them today as -- would you repeat the same under the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think I was being rather well briefed at the time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you identify for us -- I take it that most of us this is garnered from your communications with UNPROFOR personnel, perhaps even with General Rose and Colonel Shadbolt, but your description of the NATO commanders and the one who gave these words, did that also come from those contacts, or if not, could you tell us where that came from?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 18 years distance, I'm sorry, I can't remember where that phrase came from, but it certainly came from somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And was it your understanding based upon the information and the conversations that you had with people that General Rose was having a conflict with NATO because NATO envisioned using much more force against the Serbs than actually engaging in combat or warfare against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say that his critics accused him of making the same mistakes as in Munich, are we talking about critics within NATO or within the public? Could you be more specific about that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't be. All I can say is that there were misgivings among NATO officers whether this was going to work. And in the daily press conferences of UNPROFOR, the UN forces was repeatedly taken to task by journalists like Kurt Schork of Reuters for an inadequate response.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last item I'd like to look at is at page 30 in e-court of this document which will correlate to page 183 of your book. And it again relates to the Gorazde situation which we've already summarised in some detail. So I would just highlight one additional aspect. And that will be the last paragraph on the right-hand side of the page: "The cries for help from Gorazde were supplemented in Sarajevo by daily statements from the Bosnian prime minister, Haris Silajdzic, who was an easy man to like and a hard one to keep off the screen. By his mastery of the sound bite he probably did more single-handedly to affect the course of the war than anyone else except General Ratko Mladic on the Serb side: Mladic did it with guns and Silajdzic with words. The combination of his eloquence and our own exclusion from Serb-held territory meant that the Bosnian government's view of events prevailed." Now, in regards to this, sir, this is a continuation of your discussion as to Gorazde, am I correct, sir, that the Bosnian government view as to Gorazde as promulgated by Prime Minister Haris Silajdzic was the one that turned out to be a false and misrepresenting view once people got into the ground and saw what had happened in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would use the -- the words "false" and "misrepresenting" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exaggerated a bit, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think "overstated" would be fair, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Ms. Bolton, we have some 25 minutes left, 25 minutes to half an hour. We will take a break of one minute for me to be able to leave the courtroom at quarter past 2.00. Meanwhile you may start your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just with respect to that last issue of Gorazde, did I understand you to testify earlier that you never actually made it into Gorazde yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closest I got was a Serb position overlooking the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the previous passage you were asked about -- about General Rose, apparently, being on the phone and making phone calls in April 1994, was that something you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- well, no, I wouldn't -- I didn't spend my time inside his headquarters, but I knew and trusted enough people there that if they told me it was going on, it was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So that wasn't General Rose, I take it, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been. But again at this distance I don't know. He was certainly much more forthcoming with us than General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Now you were asked some questions about Arkan, and I'd just like to return to that if I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'd like to have 65 ter 10652 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You'll see, sir, from the title page of this document that it's an UNPROFOR BH command forward HQ Sarajevo office civil affairs document. It's a weekly political assessment for a period covering 28th August to, I think, 3rd of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 of this document, please. We're looking for paragraph 8. And in the B/C/S version, please, if we could go to -- forward two pages. Sorry, one more, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now you'll see at paragraph 8 there is a reference to the following: "Following continued mass expulsions of non-Serbs from the Bijeljina and Banja Luka regions this week, including 750 last night from Bijeljina, and as throughout the month of August, the Security Council issued a presidential statement demanding that the practice be stopped and that access to the area be given to international organisations. Those being expelled are normally elderly people, women and children who are forced to pay 200 Deutschmarks to cross the confrontation lines. According to reports from people who have been expelled, the man generally believed to be responsible for the atrocities in the Bijeljina area is Vojkan Djurkovic, president of the 'regional exchange commission,' and of Bijeljina chapter of Arkan's 'Party People's Choice.'" Can I ask you, sir, if you are familiar with Mr. Djurkovic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I worked in Bijeljina hardly at all, just passing through it in the early stages of the war. Of course I knew Arkan well but not him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could I ask Your Honours, first, that this document -- sorry, could I ask, please, to have video-clip 22565E played.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are other people hearing anything?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not switched on your microphone, Ms. Bolton. So therefore the French interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. We're going to try again now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Announcer: ... non-Serb civilians being expelled from Serb-held territory in the north-east of the country. Yesterday, around 800 Muslims from the town of Bijeljina were driven across the front line to government-held territory near Tuzla. If the so-called ethnic cleansing continues, no Muslims or Croats will be left in the town by the end of the week. "Martin Bell: They were rounded up near their homes in Bijeljina by Serbian militia late in the day. Robbed of their money and valuables, taken in buses and trucks, and dumped in the rain near the front line. A group of 150 men of military age who started with them were taken away, destination unknown. The hundreds who came across, women, elderly, and the infirm, had to make it on their own through several miles across the front line. A few were able to come in horse-drawn carts. It was as brutal an expulsion as any seen in more than two years of war. "Woman Refugee: The women are crying, the children are crying, the mothers are crying. All those poor people around you, you can see. What we're carrying? This is what we're carrying. Only one bag. This is all. "Martin Bell: The UN and its agencies with no significant presence in the Serb-held territory are unable to prevent the expulsion. They and International Red Cross are doing what they can to help the victims this side of the line. "Antonella Notari: We set up a first aid post at the end of the confrontation line. We have a vehicle getting the people from the first line of the confrontation line to the first aid post. We have a doctor there who is treating them and we are helping them to shuttle the people down to Babina Luka. "Martin Bell: 2.000 Muslims are known to be living still in the area around Bijeljina. The Serbian war lord responsible for this expulsion has threatened that they will all be out by Thursday. That, incidentally, is the day of the Pope's proposed visit to Bosnia. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, the French interpreters had difficulties in hearing the sound and therefore were unable to -- and the same is true for the B/C/S. I think there was no B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is, I can indicate, a transcript both -- of the B/C/S available and there is a transcript of the English available. I know that doesn't assist the French very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you provided it to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we still have a bit of a problem. Yes. And I think Mr. Mladic also did not receive any interpretation. Is that correct, Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore we can't have the witness be examined on -- we can't have the witness examined if Mr. Mladic was unable to follow what was said in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we try playing it again, Your Honour, and we could provide Mr. Mladic with a copy of the written transcript to see if that assists him in following along?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that Mr. Mladic is agreeing to such a solution. I take that from his body language, which was thumbs up and applause. And nodding as well. If I turn up the -- the English channel, I am -- it reaches a volume which is audible for me. Could we check whether there is any possibility that we have both English and B/C/S in such a way that it can be followed? I suggest that we play it again. And one thing is for certain, more attention will have to be paid in the coming days and weeks to the way we proceed with videos. Well, having the volume button now all at a maximum, could we replay the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Announcer: Relief workers in Bosnia say there has been a marked increase in the number of non-Serb civilians being expelled from Serb-held territory in the north-east of the country. They say around 800 Muslims in the town of Bijeljina were driven across the front line to government held territory near Tuzla. If so-called ethnic cleansing continues, no Muslims or Croats will be left in the town by the end of the week. "Martin Bell: They were rounded up near their homes in Bijeljina by Serbian militia late in the day. Robbed of their money and valuables, taken in buses and trucks and dumped in the rain near the front line. A group of 150 men of military age who started with them were taken away, destination unknown. The hundreds we came across, women, elderly, and the infirm had to make it on their own through several miles across the front line. A few were able to come in horse drawn carts. It was as brutal an expulsion as any we've seen in more than two years of war. "Woman Refugee: The women are crying, the children are crying, the mothers are crying. All those poor people around you, you can see. What we're carrying? This is what we're carrying. Only one bag. This is all. "Martin Bell: The UN and its agencies with no significant presence in the Serb-held territory are unable to prevent the expulsion. They and the International Red Cross are doing what they can to help the victims this side of the line. "Antonella Notari: We set up a first-aid post against the confrontation line. We have vehicles getting the people from the first line of confrontation lines to the first-aid post. We have a doctor there who is treating them and we're helping them to shuttle the people down to Babina Luka. "Martin Bell: 2.000 Muslims are known to be living still in the area around Bijeljina. The Serbian war lord responsible for this expulsion has threatened that they will all be out by Thursday. That, incidentally, is the day of the Pope's proposed visit to Bosnia. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The French translation is not complete but I think we can work on the basis of the written version of what we heard in English and of most of the French, most of the French translation having been produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Earlier today, sir, you mentioned that you thought there had been an expulsion from the Bijeljina area in 1994 in addition to the one in 1992. Is this the incident that you are referring to earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there were -- there were many similar expulsions, most of them went from Prijedor down to Turbe which is near Travnik in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You used the phrase "field security" several times today. Could you tell us what you are referring to when you are talking about field security?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to measures that armies put in place so that their operations are not compromised, their plans are not known, and information does not get into the public domain through the press or in any other way which may give -- give away positions or operations or plans to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, the Chamber will take a break of anything between half and a whole minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record show that with Judge Orie gone, the Chamber now is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Madam Bolton, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the context of questioning today on "In Harms Way," you were read a portion of a paragraph where -- a paragraph, I think it was at page 108, which included a quote about when events occurring in Sarajevo "the cameras would never be far away." Could you just comment on why that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many cameras in a fairly small area. I've defined it in previous testimonies about a mile and half from between the airport and the Turkish fort. And they would be roaming around and they would be on the spot very quickly when something happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I was a little confused on your answers about the SS Handzar movement. At page 35 of the transcript, you were asked a question about your knowledge of the Ustasha movement and the SS Handzar movement, and in answer to that question you stated: "It was the Ustasha movement that I was familiar with. And almost from the start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you would find Croats driving around with pictures of the Ustasha leader, Ante Pavlovic on the back of their car." Then at page 37 of the transcript Mr. Ivetic put to you the following question: "And now I want to ask you: In your discussions with the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership and in your discussions with the common Bosnian Serb soldier throughout the time of your stay in the region to report on the conflict going on there, did these individuals often talk to you or refer to a fear of a resurge --" I think it's supposed to be resurgence, "of the Ustasha and Handzar movements from World War II?" And you responded: "Yes, Mr. Ivetic," and then you go on. And I'm trying to understand whether you did or didn't have references made to the SS Handzar movement.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talk about only what I know about. I knew about the Ustashas so that's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You were played a portion of a video, 1D00631, and I'd like to go to the end of the portion you were played. I think Ms. Stewart has done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we're now at -- sorry, I didn't make note of the end. So we're just going to have to play. It starts at 32:52 and I believe the report goes until 35:19. I should indicate, Your Honours, that this is just something that's come up in cross-examination, so it's not something we anticipated and we haven't got a transcript available in written form at this point but we will have one prepared. Hopefully the sound is better on this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "There has been a gun battle going on around this hotel in the parkland all morning. You can probably hear it in the background. It hasn't stopped since [indiscernible]. It's quite intense. We have now been told or rather the European Community Monitors here have been warned that this place has been targeted for incoming mortar fire sometime around now. So it's not a very comfortable situation. "I can assure you from personal experience that there is no [indiscernible]. That is a hard one to say. The -- I'm sorry, it's a little bit disturbing some of this noise. The Muslims are in very difficult position geographically in that the Serbs have the high ground and the Serbs and army have them surrounded. On the other hand, the Muslims fought back strongly yesterday, and as far as I can tell what's going on here, it's a fairly -- it's a fairly even match. I think its fairly -- I think it's for certain now the Serbs are going to be bringing up some reserves which they -- which they need. They probably might have the upper-hand for longer. I'm sure [indiscernible] the Muslims are giving them a hard time --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt. Mr. Mladic can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is -- we're still on the portion which was played earlier in Court by the Defence, Your Honour. So I wonder if the issue -- if we could continue until we get to the new part and see if we can hear the new part, because this has already been MFI'd by the Defence, this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we then start at the new part? It's not necessary to replay all the parts we have seen already.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just have to find where that part ends. One moment, please. We're going to start then, Your Honours, thank you, from 35 -- no, it's ... it's -- I think we stopped at 35:19 and we're now going to continue from 35:19. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "Thirty seconds before the end of the interview when the cameraman ducked and Martin said, 'Excuse me,' a bullet went about six feet behind him and hit the wall of the hotel. You can just see a white flash on the right of screen. Martin still has the bullet."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: We do not interpret if we do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, and I'm sorry, we're actually -- the report perviously stopped at 30 -- Your Honours, I'll just deal with this by way of the bar table. It's too complicated without the transcript working. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Lastly, sir, you had indicated -- you were read a portion of your book dealing in black marketing in food and fuel and the involvement of Ukrainian Bat. First of all, are you aware of any relationship between the VRS and Ukrainian Bat concerning allegations of black-marketeering?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the passages in the book made reference to black-marketeering in Zepa, and when a UN aid convoy went into Zepa it had a Ukrainian escort. This was in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, my question was whether you were aware of the VRS being involved in terms of facilitating or benefitting from black-marketeering?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this distance, I'm sorry. I just can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are all of my questions, Your Honour. I'm wondering if we could have -- either admit the document that I used with the witness through the bar table or through the witness. That was 10562 -- no, 10652. And I'll also be seeking admission of the -- of the previous video that I played of events in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was 10652, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That was the UNPROFOR document, the civil affairs report about the events in Bijeljina in 1994 and the reports that were being received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. My recollection was that the witness said he did not know the individual mentioned in the report. I do not object to it being tendered by the bar table, but I don't think that the witness verified any of the information in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we MFI it then?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That will be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, 10652 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 10652 receives number P840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the 65 ter number for the video that was shown to the witness, Your Honour, was 22565E, and this is the video where he confirmed it was his report from events in Bijeljina in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May that be given a number, please, Madam Registrar. It's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22565E receives number P841, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, what was the exhibit number for 10652? Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number? Was it the video 22565E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 10652, the one before that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 10652, P840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Because I see it's P860 on the transcript here, so you must correct that, Mr. Stenographer. Okay. Thank you so much. Is that all, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That is it in terms of my re-examination, Your Honour. We have issues, obviously, with respect to the non-associated exhibits and the exhibits which were discussed in the witness comments chart and also the associated exhibits, but those I think could be addressed in the absence of the witness unless there is any further questioning for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we can do that not necessarily today.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've gone far beyond our time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm wondering if you want us to come back and deal with that on Monday orally or how you'd like to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I think you had better do it on a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the associated exhibits, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, not the associated exhibits. Whatever the clip that you said was complicated and you would deal with, that you can do at the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I meant the remaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The remaining things, we can deal with them orally on [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll deal with those on Monday orally then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Provided we do finish with the video conference link.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Bell, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. The Chamber takes this time to thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal and to testify in this matter and answer all the questions put to you by both Prosecution and Defence as well as the Chamber. We wish you to travel well back home. You may now stand-down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anything to wind up for the day for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we stand adjourned until Monday -- I beg your pardon, before we do that there is one little housekeeping matter here. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then we stand adjourned to Monday, the 4th of February at 9.30, in courtroom III. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
